On algebraic Stein operators for Gaussian polynomials

Ehsan Azmoodeh ††thanks: Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 7ZL, United Kingdom. E-mail: ehsan.azmoodeh@liverpool.ac.uk    Dario Gasbarra ††thanks: University of Helsinki, Department of Mathematics and Statistics, B 314, FI-00014, Finland. E-mail: dario.gasbarra@helsinki.fi    Robert E. Gaunt ††thanks: The University of Manchester, Department of Mathematics, Alan Turing Building 2.217, M13 9PL Manchester, United Kingdom. E-mail: robert.gaunt@manchester.ac.uk
Abstract

The first essential ingredient to build up Stein’s method for a continuous target distribution is to identify a so-called Stein operator, namely a linear differential operator with polynomial coefficients. In this paper, we introduce the notion of algebraic Stein operators (see Definition 3.2), and provide a novel algebraic method to find all the algebraic Stein operators up to a given order and polynomial degree for a target random variable of the form Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X), where X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{d}) has i.i.d. standard Gaussian components and h∈𝕂⁡[X]h\in\mathbb{K}[X] is a polynomial with coefficients in the ring 𝕂\mathbb{K}. Our approach links the existence of an algebraic Stein operator with null controllability of a certain linear discrete system. A MATLAB code checks the null controllability up to a given finite time TT (the order of the differential operator), and provides all null control sequences (polynomial coefficients of the differential operator) up to a given maximum degree mm. This is the first paper that connects Stein’s method with computational algebra to find Stein operators for highly complex probability distributions, such as H20​(X1)H_{20}(X_{1}), where HpH_{p} is the pp-th Hermite polynomial. Some examples of Stein operators for Hp​(X1)H_{p}(X_{1}), p=3,4,5,6p=3,4,5,6, are gathered in the Appendix and many other examples are given in the Supplementary Information.

Keywords: Stein’s method; Stein operator; Gaussian integration by parts; Malliavin calculus; linear system theory; null controllability; symbolic computation; Hermite polynomials;
MSC 2010: Primary 60H07; 93B05 Secondary 60F05

1 Introduction

We begin with the following definition that plays a pivotal role in our paper.

Definition 1.1.

Let YY be a (continuous) target random variable. We say that a linear differential operator 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t} acting on a class ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions is a polynomial Stein operator for YY if (a) 𝒮​f∈L1​(Y)\mathcal{S}f\in L^{1}(Y), (b) 𝔼⁡[𝒮​f​(Y)]=0\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{S}f(Y)\right]=0 for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, and (c) the coefficients of 𝒮\mathcal{S} are polynomial. By P​S​Oℱ​(Y)PSO_{\mathcal{F}}(Y) we denote the set of all polynomial Stein operators, acting on a class ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions, for the target random variable YY.

In the last decade, polynomial Stein operators have got a lot of attention due to their important role in the Nourdin-Peccati Malliavian–Stein approach [46, 48]. This powerful method not only provides a drastic simplification of the classical method of the moments/cumulants, but also allows for quantification of many significant probabilistic limit theorems that were not possible before. Historically, in 1972, Charles Stein [59] introduced a powerful technique for estimating the error in Gaussian approximations. Stein’s method for Gaussian approximation rests on the following fundamental Gaussian integration by parts formula: for X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1) a standard Gaussian random variable,

𝔼⁡[X​f​(X)−∂f⁡(X)]=0\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[Xf(X)-\partial f(X)\bigr]=0 (1.1)

for all absolutely continuous functions f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that 𝔼​|∂f⁡(X)|<∞\mathbb{E}|\partial f(X)|<\infty. Here ∂=dd​x\partial=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x} is the usual differentiation operator. This formula leads to the so-called Stein equation:

x​f​(x)−∂f⁡(x)=h⁡(x)−𝔼⁡[h⁡(X)],xf(x)-\partial f(x)=h(x)-\mathbb{E}[h(X)], (1.2)

where the test function hh is real-valued. It is straightforward to verify that f(x)=−ex2/2∫−∞x{h(t)−𝔼[h(X)]}e−t2/2dtf(x)=-\mathrm{e}^{x^{2}/2}\int_{-\infty}^{x}\{h(t)-\mathbb{E}[h(X)]\}\mathrm{e}^{-t^{2}/2}\,\mathrm{d}t solves (1.2), and bounds on the solution and its derivatives in terms of the test function hh and its derivatives are given in [15, 18]. Evaluating both sides of (1.2) at a random variable WW and taking expectations gives

𝔼⁡[W​f​(W)−∂f⁡(W)]=𝔼⁡[h⁡(W)]−𝔼⁡[h⁡(X)].\mathbb{E}[Wf(W)-\partial f(W)]=\mathbb{E}[h(W)]-\mathbb{E}[h(X)]. (1.3)

Thus, the problem of bounding the quantity |𝔼⁡[h⁡(W)]−𝔼⁡[h⁡(X)]||\mathbb{E}[h(W)]-\mathbb{E}[h(X)]| has been reduced to bounding the left-hand side of (1.3). A detailed account of Stein’s method for Gaussian approximation and some of its numerous applications throughout the mathematical sciences are given in the monograph [60] and the books [15, 48].

One of the advantages of Stein’s method is that the above procedure can be extended to treat many other distributional approximations. In adapting the method to a new continuous distribution, the first step is to find a suitable analogue of the integration by parts formula (1.1). For a target random variable YY, this amounts to seeking a Stein operator 𝒮\mathcal{S} acting on a class of functions ℱ\mathcal{F} such that 𝒮​f∈L1​(Y)\mathcal{S}f\in L^{1}(Y) and

𝔼⁡[𝒮​f​(Y)]=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[{\mathcal{S}}f(Y)\bigr]=0.

For continuous distributions, 𝒮\mathcal{S} is typically a differential operator, although some operators in the recent literature are integral or fractional [4, 64]. As noted by [12], for a given distribution, there are infinitely many Stein operators. A common approach to sifting through the available options is to restrict to TT-th order polynomial Stein operators (see Definition 1.1) of the form

𝒮​f​(y)=∑t=0Tpt​(y)​∂tf⁡(y)\displaystyle{\mathcal{S}}f(y)=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}(y)\partial^{t}f(y) (1.4)

in which the coefficients belongs to the polynomial ring 𝕂⁡[y]\mathbb{K}[y] in the single variable yy. (In this paper, ∂0≡I\partial^{0}\equiv I, the identity operator. For ease of exposition, we abuse notation and write yy in place of y​IyI.) In addition to their utility in the Malliavin-Stein method, such Stein operators are amenable to the various coupling techniques used in the implementation of Stein’s method to derive distributional approximations, and as such the vast majority of differential Stein operators used in the literature take this form; for an overview see [29, 42].

The density method [60, 43, 42, 61] leads to first order Stein operators, which are polynomial if the log derivative of the density is a rational function; this approach provides first order polynomial Stein operators for, amongst others, target distributions which belong to the Pearson family [58] or which satisfy a diffusive assumption [17, 40]. Another method that naturally leads to first order Stein operators is the generator method of [12, 32]. However, it is often necessary to consider higher order operators; second order polynomial operators are needed for the Laplace [55], PRR [54] and variance-gamma [25] distributions, for example. This is because the densities of these distributions satisfy second order differential equations with polynomial coefficients. In recent years, techniques have been developed for obtaining Stein operators in increasingly complex settings, such as the iterated conditioning argument for deriving Stein operators for products of a quite general class of distributions [26, 27, 29, 30] and the Fourier/Malliavin calculus approach used to obtain Stein operators for linear combinations of gamma random variables [2, 3].

However, there remain many important distributional limits for which Stein’s method has not yet been adapted to. One identified by [53] to be of particular importance are those of the form P⁡(X)P(X), where X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1) and PP is a polynomial of degree strictly greater than 2. The case in which PP is the pp-th Hermite polynomial, Hp(x)=(−1)pex2/2∂d(e−x2/2)H_{p}(x)=(-1)^{p}\mathrm{e}^{x^{2}/2}\partial^{d}(\mathrm{e}^{-x^{2}/2}), is of particular interest, due to their fundamental role in Gaussian analysis and Malliavin calculus. More importantly, they appear as the natural target distributions in the classic asymptotic theory of UU-statistics, see [39, Section 4.4] and [41, Chapter 3]. For example, it is well-known that by taking the kernel ψ⁡(x1,…,xp)=x1​x2​…​xp\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{p})=x_{1}x_{2}\ldots x_{p}, the limit of the corresponding UU-statistics is Hp​(X)H_{p}(X), see page 87 in the latter reference. Indeed, since the seminal paper [46], the Malliavin-Stein method has been used to derive numerous quantitative limits theorems for a wide class of laws (see, for example, [20, 21]), and has been particularly successful in the case that the target distribution is an element of the first or second Wiener chaos (see, for example, [2, 5, 7, 9, 19, et15, 45, 46, 50, 49, 51]), but little is known regarding convergence to targets from higher order chaoses. In the Stein’s method literature, the only contribution is the modest one of [28] in which elementary but involved manipulations were used to obtain fifth and third order polynomial Stein operators for the target distributions H3​(X)H_{3}(X) and H4​(X)H_{4}(X), respectively, which represents a first step towards the long term goal of using the Malliavin-Stein method to understand convergence towards elements of higher order Wiener chaoses. In this paper we make progress that far exceeds that of [28].

In this work, we consider the multivariate Gaussian polynomial Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X), where X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{d}) has independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) standard Gaussian components and h∈𝕂⁡[X]=𝕂⁡[X1,…,Xd]h\in\mathbb{K}[X]=\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\dots,X_{d}], 𝕂=ℤ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{Z}, ℚ\mathbb{Q}, or ℝ\mathbb{R}. For any target random variable Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) of the above form, we show, in the formalism of linear system theory, that in Gaussian space, finding Stein operators of the type (1.4) with polynomial coefficients pt​(y)∈𝕂​[Y]p_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[Y] is equivalent to solving a null controllability problem.

Controllability is a fundamental concept in mathematical control theory. Consider a (finite-dimensional) discrete-time linear time-invariant system xk+1=A​xk+B​ukx_{k+1}=Ax_{k}+Bu_{k}, k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} where x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the state, u∈ℝmu\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is the input, and AA and BB are matrices of suitable size. The controllability property of such a system refers to the fact that any initial state can be steered to any final state by choosing the input appropriately. This notion was introduced by [35] and was extensively studied by Kalman himself and many others; see [36, 34, son98] and the survey [38]. Controllability has many applications in control theory and systems theory, as well as industrial and chemical process control, reactor control, control of electric bulk power systems, aerospace engineering and quantum systems theory.

The significance of formulating the problem of finding polynomial Stein operators for Gaussian polynomials as a null controllability lies in the fact that there the problem of determining the controllability of a discrete-time linear system is well understood in the literature. The classical Kalman’s rank test rank[BAB⋯An−1B]=n\mathrm{rank}[B\,AB\,\cdots\,A^{n-1}B]=n is a necessary and sufficient for the controllability of a linear finite dimensional discrete system. An alternative characterisation, which is sometimes called the Popov-Belevitch-Hautus (PBH) test, presents an equivalent condition in terms of the eigenmodes of the system [1, 13]. In Remark 3.5, we present the algorithm used in this paper for finding a null control sequence of a discrete-time linear system that can be implemented efficiently in modern computer algebra packages.

In Definition 3.2, we introduce the notion of algebraic Stein operators, a subclass of the class of polynomial Stein operators, which in fact coincides with the class of polynomial Stein operators in the case d=1d=1 (see Proposition 3.2). For a given target Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X), the above procedure can be implemented as an algorithm in modern computer algebra packages that can find all algebraic Stein operators for Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) up to a given order TT and maximal degree of polynomial coefficients m=max0≤t≤T⁡deg⁡(pt​(y))m=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\mathrm{deg}(p_{t}(y)). We provide an efficient MATLAB code that is available to the research community at https://github.com/gasbarra/Algebraic-Stein-Equations.

In dimension d=1d=1, we use the method to study the Stein operators for targets Y=Hp​(X)Y=H_{p}(X). The ‘simplest’ Stein operators for p=1,…,6p=1,\dots,6 are displayed in Appendix D. The Supplementary Information contains many more examples. For p≥7p\geq 7, the numerical coefficients in the Stein operators become too large to present in this paper, but we give some useful summaries of these Stein operators in Table 1. It should be clear that, apart from the first few cases, it would be very hard to derive these Stein operators solely by bare-hands heroic calculations. This paper therefore constitutes not only the first connection between Stein’s method and control theory, but also the first study that deeply connects Stein’s method with computer algebra programming to find Stein operators for highly complex probability distributions, such as H20​(X)H_{20}(X).

In addition to being able to find Stein operators that are out of reach of existing methods, our connection between Stein’s method and null controllability has a feature not seen before in the Stein’s method literature. As our algorithm finds all algebraic Stein operators for a given target distribution Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) up to a given order TT and polynomial degree mm, we have confidence (at least in the case d=1d=1) as to what polynomial Stein operators for that distribution are ‘simplest’ in the sense of having minimal order TT or polynomial degree mm. For example, by running our MATLAB code to obtain polynomial Stein operators for H3​(X)H_{3}(X) and H4​(X)H_{4}(X) we know (with the aid of Proposition 4.1) that the fifth and third order operators that [28] obtained (see (D.2) and (D.3)) are ‘simplest’ in the sense of having minimum possible maximal degree 2 and have the minimum possible order TT for such operators, which was not obvious from the analysis of [28]. The complexity of Stein operators for Hp​(X)H_{p}(X) only increases as pp increases (see Table 1), with the implication being that there is a significant increase in difficulty in applying the Malliavin-Stein method for target distributions Hp​(X)H_{p}(X) for p≥3p\geq 3. Another insight we gain from the outputs of our algorithm is that for p≥3p\geq 3 there is not a unique ‘simplest’ Stein operator in that the Stein operator with smallest possible order TT (degree mm) does not have smallest possible maximal polynomial degree mm (order TT). It remains to be seen whether the Stein operators with minimal order TT or minimal degree mm are more tractable when used in the Malliavin-Stein method. Finally, we stress that the method of converting the problem of finding Stein operators into a null controllability problem applies more generally than even the Gaussian polynomial setting detailed in this paper. We expect this to be explored in future research.

We end this introduction by acknowledging that the focus of this paper is on finding Stein operators for Gaussian polynomials, but for sake of a focused treatment, we neglect the important question as to whether the Stein operators we obtain are characterising. This is the subject of our recent paper [8].

The rest of our paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, we review some fundamental Malliavin calculus operators and formulas on 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] that are needed in the paper. Section 3 constitutes the heart of the paper. In Section 3.1, we introduce the notion of a Stein chain, and make a connection between the existence of a Stein chain and polynomial Stein operators for Gaussian polynomials. We present a method for validating Stein chains in Section 3.2. In Section 3.3, we formulate the problem of finding Stein operators for Gaussian polynomials as a null controllability problem. A concise description of the implementation of the null controllability approach in MATLAB is given in the Supplementary Information (SI). In Section 4, we focus on applications to the important case of Gaussian Hermite polynomials Hp​(X)H_{p}(X), X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). We provide a detailed description of the highest order coefficient of polynomial Stein operators for Hp​(X)H_{p}(X) in Section 4.1. In Section 4.2, we summarise some interesting features of the Stein operators for Hp​(X)H_{p}(X) that are obtained by our MATLAB code; examples of the Stein operators are given Appendix D and the SI. Finally, an auxiliary lemma is stated and proved in Appendix B.

Note on the class of functions ℱ\mathcal{F}: Consider the polynomial Stein operator 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt(y)∂t\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}(y)\partial^{t}, with max0≤t≤T⁡deg⁡(pt​(y))=m\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\mathrm{deg}(p_{t}(y))=m, for the target random variable YY, supported on I⊆ℝI\subseteq\mathbb{R}. In this paper, the class of functions on which our polynomial Stein operators act is the class ℱ𝒮,Y\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{S},Y}, which is defined to be the set of all functions f∈CT​(I)f\in C^{T}(I) such that 𝔼​|Yj​f(t)​(Y)|<∞\mathbb{E}|Y^{j}f^{(t)}(Y)|<\infty for all t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T and j=0,…,mj=0,\ldots,m. To ease notation, we write P​S​O​(Y)PSO(Y) as shorthand for P​S​Oℱ𝒮,Y​(Y)PSO_{\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{S},Y}}(Y). We do not claim that this is the largest class of functions on which the Stein operators of this paper act, but the class is large enough for practical purposes and guarantees that in all of our proofs the crucial property 𝔼⁡[𝒮​f​(Y)]=0\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{S}f(Y)]=0, ∀f∈ℱ\forall f\in\mathcal{F}, holds. We also highlight that when the target random variable YY admits all moments (this is the case for all Gaussian polynomials Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X)), the class ℱ\mathcal{F} of functions as described above contains the class Cc∞​(ℝ)C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}) of infinitely differentiable functions with compact support.

2 Malliavin operators on 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}]

For the scope of our paper, it is enough to define Malliavin calculus operators on 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] (see below for definitions) algebraically, without discussing their functional analytic extensions. For a state-of-the-art exposition of Malliavin calculus in full generality see [48, 52].

2.1 Algebraic preliminaries

We denote by 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] the commutative ring of polynomials in the variables x1,…,xdx_{1},\dots,x_{d} with coefficients in 𝕂\mathbb{K}, equipped with the usual addition and multiplication.

Definition 2.1 (Ideal).

A subset J⊆𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]J\subseteq\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] is an ideal when

  1. 1.

    g1,g2∈J⟹(g1+g2)∈Jg_{1},g_{2}\in J\Longrightarrow(g_{1}+g_{2})\in J;

  2. 2.

    f∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd],g∈J⟹f​g∈Jf\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}],\;g\in J\Longrightarrow fg\in J.

Definition 2.2.

The ideal generated by A⊆𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]A\subseteq\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] is the smallest ideal of 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] containing AA, denoted by

⟨A⟩=⋂ ideal ​J⊃AJ={∑ℓ=1nfℓgℓ:fℓ∈𝕂[x1,…,xd],gℓ∈A,n∈ℕ}.\displaystyle\langle A\rangle=\bigcap_{\mbox{ ideal }J\supset A}J=\biggl\{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}f_{\ell}g_{\ell}:f_{\ell}\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}],\,g_{\ell}\in A,\,n\in\mathbb{N}\biggr\}.

When J=⟨g1,…,gn⟩J=\langle g_{1},\dots,g_{n}\rangle we say that the ideal is finitely generated.

Remark 2.1.

The ring 𝕂⁡[x1]\mathbb{K}[x_{1}] is a principal ideal domain, meaning that every ideal I⊆𝕂⁡[x1]I\subseteq\mathbb{K}[x_{1}] is principal (can be generated by one element). This useful fact gives a precise description of the structure of the highest order polynomial coefficients in Stein operators, see Proposition 4.1.

2.2 One-dimensional case

The major application of our algebraic method is to present Stein operators for univariate Gaussian Hermite polynomials. We start with a purely algebraic presentation of Malliavin operators in dimension d=1d=1.

In the univariate case, the Malliavin derivative DD, the divergence δ\delta and its pseudo-inverse δ−1\delta^{-1} are defined as linear mappings acting on the polynomial ring 𝕂⁡[x]=𝕂⁡[x1]\mathbb{K}[x]=\mathbb{K}[x_{1}], with

Dxn=∂xn=nxn−1,δxn=(x−∂)xn=xn+1−nxn−1,and\displaystyle Dx^{n}=\partial x^{n}=nx^{n-1},\quad\delta x^{n}=(x-\partial)x^{n}=x^{n+1}-nx^{n-1},\quad\text{and}
δ−1​1=0,δ−1​x=1,δ−1​xn=xn−1+(n−1)​δ−1​xn−2=∑k=0⌊n−12⌋(n−1)!!(n−1−2​k)!!​xn−1−2​k,\displaystyle\delta^{-1}1=0,\quad\delta^{-1}x=1,\quad\delta^{-1}x^{n}=x^{n-1}+(n-1)\delta^{-1}x^{n-2}=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\rfloor}\frac{(n-1){!}{!}}{(n-1-2k){!}{!}}x^{n-1-2k},

where n!!n{!}{!} denotes the double factorial.

Proposition 2.1.

Let n∈ℕ0n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. It holds that δ−1​δ​xn=xn\delta^{-1}\delta x^{n}=x^{n}. Moreover,

δ​δ−1​xn=xn−𝔼⁡[Xn],\delta\delta^{-1}x^{n}=x^{n}-\mathbb{E}\left[X^{n}\right],

where X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1) has moment sequence 𝔼⁡[Xn]=(n−1)!!\mathbb{E}\left[X^{n}\right]=(n-1){!}{!} when n∈2​ℕn\in 2\mathbb{N} and 𝔼⁡[Xn]=0\mathbb{E}\left[X^{n}\right]=0 otherwise.

Lemma 2.1 (Gaussian integration by parts).

Let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). For f,g∈𝕂⁡[x]f,g\in\mathbb{K}[x],

𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)​D​g​(X)]=𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)​∂g⁡(X)]=𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)​δ​f​(X)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[f(X)Dg(X)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[f(X)\partial g(X)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(X)\delta f(X)\bigr].
Proof.

By linearity, it suffices to consider the monomials f⁡(x)=xn,f(x)=x^{n}, g⁡(x)=xmg(x)=x^{m}. We have

𝔼[XnDXm]=(m−1)𝔼[Xn+m−1]={(n+m−2)!!​(m−1),(n+m)​ odd, 0,(n+m)​ even, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[X^{n}DX^{m}\bigr]=(m-1)\mathbb{E}\bigl[X^{n+m-1}\bigr]=\left\{\begin{matrix}(n+m-2){!}{!}(m-1),&(n+m)\mbox{ odd, }\\ 0,&(n+m)\mbox{ even, }\\ \end{matrix}\right.

which coincides with 𝔼⁡[Xm​δ​Xn]=𝔼⁡[Xm+n+1]−n​𝔼​[Xm+n−1].\mathbb{E}\left[X^{m}\delta X^{n}\right]=\mathbb{E}[X^{m+n+1}]-n\mathbb{E}[X^{m+n-1}]. ∎

Definition 2.4.

We define the univariate Hermite polynomials as H0​(x)=1H_{0}(x)=1, H1​(x)=xH_{1}(x)=x, and

Hn​(x)=δ​Hn−1​(x)=(δn​1)​(x),n≥2.H_{n}(x)=\delta H_{n-1}(x)=\bigl(\delta^{n}1\bigr)(x),\quad n\geq 2.
Proposition 2.2 (Properties of Hermite polynomials).
  1. 1.

    H0​(x),…,Hn​(x)H_{0}(x),\dots,H_{n}(x) are monic polynomials spanning 𝕂n​[x]\mathbb{K}_{n}[x] (the ring of polynomials of maximum degree nn).

  4. 4.

    For n≥1n\geq 1, D​Hn​(x)=∂Hn​(x)=n​Hn−1​(x)DH_{n}(x)=\partial H_{n}(x)=nH_{n-1}(x).

  5. 5.

    For every 0≤m≤n0\leq m\leq n, and X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1),

    𝔼⁡[Xn​Hm​(X)]=𝟏​((n−m)∈2​ℕ)​n!​(n−m−1)!!(n−m)!.\mathbb{E}\bigl[X^{n}H_{m}(X)\bigr]={\bf 1}((n-m)\in 2\mathbb{N})\frac{n!(n-m-1){!}{!}}{(n-m)!}.
Definition 2.5.

For a given (target) polynomial y=h⁡(x)y=h(x), with h∈𝕂⁡[x]h\in\mathbb{K}[x], we introduce the linear operator Γy\Gamma_{y} acting on 𝕂⁡[x]\mathbb{K}[x] as

Γy​(f⁡(x))=D​h​(x)​δ−1​(f⁡(x))=∂h⁡(x)​δ−1​(f⁡(x))∈⟨∂h⁡(x)⟩.\Gamma_{y}(f(x))=Dh(x)\delta^{-1}(f(x))=\partial h(x)\delta^{-1}(f(x))\in\big\langle\partial h(x)\big\rangle. (2.1)
Lemma 2.2.

Let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). Consider Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) where h∈𝕂⁡[x]h\in\mathbb{K}[x]. Assume that f,g∈𝕂⁡[x]f,g\in\mathbb{K}[x]. Then

𝔼⁡[g⁡(Y)​f​(X)]−𝔼⁡[g⁡(Y)]​𝔼​[f⁡(X)]=𝔼⁡[∂g⁡(Y)​ΓY​(f⁡(X))].\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Y)f(X)\bigr]-\mathbb{E}[g(Y)]\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\partial g(Y)\Gamma_{Y}(f(X))\bigr].
Proof.

Using Gaussian integration by parts formula Lemma 2.1, we can write

𝔼⁡[g⁡(Y)​f​(X)]−𝔼⁡[g⁡(Y)]​𝔼​[f⁡(X)]=𝔼⁡[g⁡(h⁡(X))​δ​δ−1​(f⁡(X))]=𝔼⁡[∂(g∘h)​(X)​δ−1​f​(X)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Y)f(X)\bigr]-\mathbb{E}[g(Y)]\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(h(X))\delta\delta^{-1}(f(X))\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\partial(g\circ h)(X)\delta^{-1}f(X)\bigr]

∎

2.3 Multidimensional case

Definition 2.6.

In the multivariate setting, we define the Malliavin operators as follows. (a) The Malliavin derivative maps a polynomial g∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]g\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\dots,x_{d}] into its gradient:

D∙​g=(Dk​g)1≤k≤d=∇g=(∂x1g⁡(x1,…,xd),…,∂xdg⁡(x1,…,xd))∈𝕂​[x1,…,xd]d.D_{\bullet}g=(D_{k}g)_{1\leq k\leq d}=\nabla g=(\partial_{x_{1}}g(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}),\dots,\partial_{x_{d}}g(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}))\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\dots,x_{d}]^{d}.

(b) The divergence δ\delta maps in the opposite direction a polynomial vector f⁡(x)=f∙​(x1,…,xd)=(f1​(x1,…,xd),…,fd​(x1,…,xd))∈𝕂​[x1,…,xd]df(x)=f_{\bullet}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})=(f_{1}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}),\dots,f_{d}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}))\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\dots,x_{d}]^{d} into the polynomial

δ​f∙​(x)=∑k=1dδk​fk​(x)=∑k=1d(fk​(x)​xk−∂xkfk​(x))∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd],\delta f_{\bullet}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\delta_{k}f_{k}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\bigl(f_{k}(x)x_{k}-\partial_{x_{k}}f_{k}(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\dots,x_{d}],

where δk\delta_{k} denotes the univariate divergence operator operating on the kk-th coordinate.

Proposition 2.3.

For X∼N⁡(0,Id)X\sim N(0,I_{d}), a standard dd-dimensional Gaussian random vector with covariance matrix the d×dd\times d identity matrix IdI_{d}, we have the multivariate Gaussian integration by parts formula

𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)​δ​f∙​(X)]=𝔼⁡[(D∙​g​(X),f∙​(X))ℝd].\mathbb{E}\big[g(X)\delta f_{\bullet}(X)\big]=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(D_{\bullet}g(X),f_{\bullet}(X)\big)_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Big].

Here, and elsewhere, (⋅,⋅)ℝd(\cdot,\cdot)_{\mathbb{R}^{d}} denotes the usual inner product on Euclidean space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

In order to define a pseudo-inverse of δ\delta in the multivariate setting, we use the multivariate Hermite polynomials instead of the monomial basis.

Definition 2.7.

(a) The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator, which maps 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\dots,x_{d}] into itself, is defined as L:=−δ​DL:=-\delta D.
(b) For a dd-dimensional multi-index α=(α1,…,αd)∈ℕ0d\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d})\in\mathbb{N}^{d}_{0}, the multivariate Hermite polynomials

Hα​(x)=Hα​(x1,…,xd)=∏k=1dHαk​(xk)H_{\alpha}(x)=H_{\alpha}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})=\prod_{k=1}^{d}H_{\alpha_{k}}(x_{k})

are eigenfunctions of LL with respective eigenvalues −|α|:=−∑k=1dαk-|\alpha|:=-\sum_{k=1}^{d}\alpha_{k}. It also follows that 𝔼⁡[Hα​(X)​Hβ​(X)]=𝟏​(α=β)​∏k=1dαk!\mathbb{E}\bigl[H_{\alpha}(X)H_{\beta}(X)\bigr]={\bf 1}(\alpha=\beta)\prod_{k=1}^{d}\alpha_{k}!.
(c) The linear mapping L−1L^{-1} operates on the multivariate Hermite polynomials as

L−1Hα(x)={0, when ​|α|=0,−|α|−1​Hα​(x),otherwise.\displaystyle L^{-1}H_{\alpha}(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix}0,&\mbox{ when }|\alpha|=0,\\ -|\alpha|^{-1}H_{\alpha}(x),&\mbox{otherwise.}\end{matrix}\right.

(d) A pseudo-inverse of δ\delta is defined as δ−1=−D​L−1\delta^{-1}=-DL^{-1}, with δ−1​1=0\delta^{-1}1=0, and, for |α|>0|\alpha|>0,

δ−1​Hα​(x)=|α|−1​D​Hα​(x)=(α1|α|​Hα−e1​(x),…,αd|α|​Hα−ed​(x)),\delta^{-1}H_{\alpha}(x)=|\alpha|^{-1}DH_{\alpha}(x)=\biggl(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{|\alpha|}H_{\alpha-e_{1}}(x),\dots,\frac{\alpha_{d}}{|\alpha|}H_{\alpha-e_{d}}(x)\biggr),

where as usual (ei:i=1,…,d)(e_{i}:i=1,\ldots,d) denote the standard basis for the Euclidean space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. It follows by definition that δ​δ−1​Hα​(x)=Hα​(x)​𝟏​(|α|>0)\delta\delta^{-1}H_{\alpha}(x)=H_{\alpha}(x){\bf 1}(|\alpha|>0).

Definition 2.8.

The nn-th polynomial chaos in the variables x1,…,xdx_{1},\dots,x_{d} is the linear subspace ℍn​[x]=ℍn​[x1,…,xd]⊆𝕂n​[x]=𝕂n​[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{H}_{n}[x]=\mathbb{H}_{n}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}]\subseteq\mathbb{K}_{n}[x]=\mathbb{K}_{n}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}] generated by the multivariate Hermite polynomials Hα​(x)H_{\alpha}(x) with |α|=n|\alpha|=n, and the decomposition

𝕂n​[x]=𝕂+ℍ1​[x]+⋯+ℍn​[x]\mathbb{K}_{n}[x]=\mathbb{K}+\mathbb{H}_{1}[x]+\dots+\mathbb{H}_{n}[x]

is orthogonal with respect to the dd-dimensional standard Gaussian measure.

Definition 2.9.

In the multivariate case, with (target) polynomial y=h⁡(x1,…,xd)y=h(x_{1},\dots,x_{d}), and h∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]h\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}], we define the linear Gamma operator Γy\Gamma_{y} as: (x=(x1,…,xd))(x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}))

Γy​(f⁡(x))=(D​y,δ−1​f​(x))ℝd=(D​h​(x),−D​L−1​f​(x))ℝd.\Gamma_{y}(f(x))=\bigl(Dy,\delta^{-1}f(x)\bigr)_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}=\bigl(Dh(x),-DL^{-1}f(x)\bigr)_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}. (2.2)

For example, Γy​(1)=0\Gamma_{y}(1)=0 and for a multivariate Hermite polynomial

Γy​(Hα​(x))=∑k=1dαk|α|​Hα−ek​(x)​∂xkh⁡(x).\displaystyle\Gamma_{y}(H_{\alpha}(x))=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\frac{\alpha_{k}}{|\alpha|}H_{\alpha-e_{k}}(x)\partial_{x_{k}}h(x).

Note that Γy\Gamma_{y} maps 𝕂⁡[x]\mathbb{K}[x] into the ideal ⟨∇h​(x)⟩=⟨∂x1h⁡(x),…,∂xdh⁡(x)⟩\langle\nabla h(x)\rangle=\big\langle\partial_{x_{1}}h(x),\dots,\partial_{x_{d}}h(x)\big\rangle generated by the gradient of the target polynomial.

Lemma 2.3.

For X=(X1,…,Xd)∼N⁡(0,Id)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\sim N(0,I_{d}), Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X), with h∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]h\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}], and every f∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd],g∈𝕂⁡[Y]f\in\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}],g\in\mathbb{K}[Y],

𝔼⁡[g⁡(Y)​f​(X)]=𝔼⁡[g⁡(Y)]​𝔼​[f⁡(X)]+𝔼⁡[∂g⁡(Y)​ΓY​(f⁡(X))].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[g(Y)f(X)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[g(Y)]\mathbb{E}[f(X)]+\mathbb{E}\bigl[\partial g(Y)\Gamma_{Y}(f(X))\bigr]. (2.3)

3 An algebraic formalism of Stein operators

Throughout this section, we adapt the following setting. Let d≥1d\geq 1. Assume X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}), where X1,…,XdX_{1},\ldots,X_{d} are i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables. Choose a polynomial h∈𝕂⁡[x]=𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]h\in\mathbb{K}[x]=\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}]. We consider a polynomial target random variable YY in the Gaussian variates, namely that,

Y=h⁡(X)=h⁡(X1,…,Xd).Y=h(X)=h(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}). (3.1)

Without loss of generality, we also assume that I​E​[Y]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Y]=0 (this assumption is always possible with a shift). Furthermore, the set 𝕂⁡[y]≅𝕂⁡[h⁡(x)]\mathbb{K}[y]\cong\mathbb{K}[h(x)] of all polynomials in the variable yy composed with the target polynomial h⁡(x)h(x) is a subring of 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xd]\mathbb{K}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}]. Denote by H⁡(Y)=L2​(Ω,σ⁡(Y),γd)H(Y)=L^{2}(\Omega,\sigma(Y),\gamma_{d}) the Hilbert space of all YY-measurable, square integrable random variables with respect to the dd-dimensional standard Gaussian measure γd\gamma_{d}. Also, H​(Y)⟂H(Y)^{\perp} stands for the orthogonal complement of H⁡(Y)H(Y).

3.1 Forward Stein chain

We begin with the notion of a Stein chain. Our definition is quite abstract, but simply speaking, a Stein chain for the target random variable YY is the sequence of polynomial coefficients of a Stein operator for YY (when it exists); hence its name. This connection is made in Proposition 3.1. A benefit of this abstract definition is that it allows us to define the notation of an algebraic Stein chain in a natural manner. The distinction between general and algebraic Stein chains is important, because Stein operators whose polynomial coefficients form an algebraic Stein chain are easier to find; see Remark 3.2, item (i).

Definition 3.1 (Forward Stein chain).

Suppose that the target random variable YY has the Gaussian polynomial form given by relation (3.1).

  • (a)

    A (general) Stein chain of length T≥1T\geq 1 for YY is a sequence (pt(y)∈𝕂[y]:t=0,…,T)(p_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]:t=0,\ldots,T) such that: gT+pT​(Y)∈H​(Y)⟂g_{T}+p_{T}(Y)\in H(Y)^{\perp} where the sequence of Gaussian polynomials g=(gt∈𝕂[X1,…,Xd]:t=0,…,T)g=(g_{t}\in\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}]:t=0,\ldots,T) is recursively defined via

    g0\displaystyle g_{0} =0,\displaystyle=0,
    gt\displaystyle g_{t} =ΓY(gt−1+pt−1(Y)),t=1,…,T,\displaystyle=\Gamma_{Y}(g_{t-1}+p_{t-1}(Y)),\quad t=1,\ldots,T, (3.2)

    where the Malliavin Gamma mapping ΓY\Gamma_{Y} is defined in (2.1) and (2.2) when d=1d=1 and d≥2d\geq 2, respectively, and moreover I​E​[gt]=−I​E​[pt​(Y)]{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{t}]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{t}(Y)] for t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T. Let S​C​(Y,T)SC(Y,T) denote the set of all Stein chains of length TT, and let S​C​(Y)=⋃T≥1S​C​(Y,T)SC(Y)=\bigcup_{T\geq 1}SC(Y,T) stand for the set of all Stein chains of finite length.

  • (b)

    An algebraic Stein chain of length T≥1T\geq 1 for YY is a Stein chain (pt(y)∈𝕂[y]:t=0,…,T)(p_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]:t=0,\ldots,T) such that: gT+pT​(Y)∈{0}g_{T}+p_{T}(Y)\in\{0\} almost surely. Let A​S​C​(Y,T)ASC(Y,T) denote the set of all algebraic Stein chains of length TT, and let A​S​C​(Y)=⋃T≥1S​C​(Y,T)ASC(Y)=\bigcup_{T\geq 1}SC(Y,T) stand for the set of all algebraic Stein chains of finite length.

Remark 3.1.
  1. (i)

    The moment property I​E​[gt]=−I​E​[pt​(Y)]{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{t}]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{t}(Y)] for t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T in Definition 3.1 is immaterial, and can always be assumed due the fact that the linear map ΓY\Gamma_{Y} does not see constants, namely, ΓY​(f⁡(X)+c)=ΓY​(f⁡(X))\Gamma_{Y}(f(X)+c)=\Gamma_{Y}(f(X)) for any constant cc.

  2. (ii)

    We stress that the subring 𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{K}[Y] is not stable under the linear mapping ΓY\Gamma_{Y}, meaning ΓY​(𝕂⁡[Y])⊈𝕂⁡[Y]\Gamma_{Y}(\mathbb{K}[Y])\nsubseteq\mathbb{K}[Y]. For example, a common candidate – from the Malliavin-Stein perspective – for the first polynomial entry in the Stein chain is p0​(Y)=c​Yp_{0}(Y)=cY, c∈𝕂c\in\mathbb{K}. It can be readily seen that with the choices Y=Hp​(X)Y=H_{p}(X), p≥3p\geq 3, and p0​(Y)=c​Yp_{0}(Y)=cY we have g1∉𝕂⁡[Y]g_{1}\notin\mathbb{K}[Y]. Therefore, the most notable feature of a Stein chain or an algebraic Stein chain is that the final output of the linear machine (3.2), either conditionally on the target variable YY or without, is an element in the subring 𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{K}[Y].

  3. (iii)

    Note that by the definition of the ΓY\Gamma_{Y} operator, all the intermediate Gaussian polynomials

    gt=gt(X1,…,Xd)∈⟨∇h(X1,…,Xd)⟩,∀t=0,…,T.g_{t}=g_{t}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\in\big\langle\nabla h(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\big\rangle,\quad\forall\,t=0,\ldots,T.

    More importantly, when the Stein chain is algebraic, gT∈𝕂⁡[Y]∩⟨∇h​(X1,…,Xd)⟩g_{T}\in\mathbb{K}[Y]\cap\langle\nabla h(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\rangle. On the other hand, I=𝕂⁡[Y]∩⟨∇h​(X1,…,Xd)⟩I=\mathbb{K}[Y]\cap\langle\nabla h(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\rangle is an ideal of the subring 𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{K}[Y], and therefore it can be generated by one element (see Remark 2.1). In dimension d=1d=1, for the targets of the form of a Gaussian Hermite polynomial, we present a prototypical element that generates the corresponding ideal, see Proposition 4.1 for details.

Let us continue with the following basic fact that tells us that the existence of a Stein chain of length TT, in a natural way, leads to a polynomial Stein operator of order TT for the target random variable YY.

Proposition 3.1.

Suppose that all the assumptions of Definition 3.1 prevail. Then, the following statements hold:

  • (a)

    For every T≥1T\geq 1, A​S​C​(Y,T)⊆S​C​(Y,T)ASC(Y,T)\subseteq SC(Y,T). Moreover, A​S​C​(Y)⊆S​C​(Y)ASC(Y)\subseteq SC(Y).

  • (b)

    Let (pt(y)∈𝕂[y]:t=0,…,T)(p_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]\,:\,t=0,\ldots,T) be a forward Stein chain for the target random variable YY. Then 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈PSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in PSO(Y). Conversely, if 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈PSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in PSO(Y), then the sequence of polynomials (pt(y)∈𝕂[y]:t=0,…,T)∈SC(Y,T)(p_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]\,:\,t=0,\ldots,T)\in SC(Y,T) is a forward Stein chain for YY of length TT.

Proof.

(a) This is clear because 0∈H​(Y)⟂0\in H(Y)^{\perp}. (b) Using iteratively the integration by parts formula (2.3), along with the moment property I​E​[gt+pt​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{t}+p_{t}(Y)]=0, for t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T, in Definition 3.1 (in particular, I​E​[p0​(Y)]=g0=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(Y)]=g_{0}=0), for every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, we can write

I​E​[(p0​(Y)−I​E​[p0​(Y)])​f​(Y)]=I​E​[∂f⁡(Y)​ΓY​(p0​(Y)+g0)⏟g1]=\displaystyle{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\biggl[\bigl(p_{0}(Y)-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(Y)]\bigr)f(Y)\biggr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\biggl[\partial f(Y)\underbrace{\Gamma_{Y}\bigl(p_{0}(Y)+g_{0}\bigr)}_{g_{1}}\biggr]=
−IE[p1(Y)∂f(Y)]+IE[∂2f(Y)ΓY​(p1​(Y)+g1)⏟g2]=\displaystyle-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigr[p_{1}(Y)\partial f(Y)\bigr]+{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\biggl[\partial^{2}f(Y)\underbrace{\Gamma_{Y}(p_{1}(Y)+g_{1}\bigr)}_{g_{2}}\biggr]=
−I​E​[p1​(Y)​∂f⁡(Y)]−I​E​[p2​(Y)​∂2f⁡(Y)]−⋯−I​E​[pT−1​(Y)​∂T−1f⁡(Y)]\displaystyle-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{1}(Y)\partial f(Y)\bigr]-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{2}(Y)\partial^{2}f(Y)\bigr]-\dots-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{T-1}(Y)\partial^{T-1}f(Y)\bigr]
+I​E​[∂Tf⁡(Y)​OPENΓY​(pT−1​(Y)+gT−1))⏟gT].\displaystyle+{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\biggl[\partial^{T}f(Y)\underbrace{\Gamma_{Y}\bigl(p_{T-1}(Y)+g_{T-1}\bigr)\bigr)}_{g_{T}}\biggr].

Hence, I​E​[∑t=0Tpt​(Y)​∂tf⁡(Y)]=I​E​[p0​(Y)]​I​E​[f⁡(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}(Y)\partial^{t}f(Y)\bigr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(Y)]{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[f(Y)]=0, and therefore, the operator 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t} is a polynomial Stein operator for the target random variable YY. For the other direction, let 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈PSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in PSO(Y) be a polynomial Stein operator for YY. Then the condition I​E​[𝒮​f​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[\mathcal{S}f(Y)]=0 for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} together with an iterative use of the integration by parts formula yields that I​E​[∂Tf⁡(Y)​(pT​(Y)+gT)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[\partial^{T}f(Y)\left(p_{T}(Y)+g_{T}\right)\right]=0 for every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}. Hence, using a standard density argument we can conclude that I​E​[pT​(Y)+gT|Y]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[p_{T}(Y)+g_{T}\,|\,Y\right]=0, and so gT+pT​(Y)∈H​(Y)⟂g_{T}+p_{T}(Y)\in H(Y)^{\perp}. ∎

Proposition 3.1, item (b), provides a neat correspondence between P​S​O​(Y)PSO(Y) and S​C​(Y)SC(Y). This useful fact in addition to the novel notion of an algebraic Stein chain introduced in Definition 3.1, item (b), directs us to the notion of an algebraic polynomial Stein operator that is the cornerstone of our paper.

Definition 3.2 (Algebraic polynomial Stein operator).

Let d≥1d\geq 1, and suppose that the target random variable YY has the Gaussian polynomial form given by relation (3.1). Let T≥1T\geq 1, and 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈PSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in PSO(Y). We say that 𝒮\mathcal{S} is an algebraic polynomial Stein operator of length TT for target random variable YY when the sequence of polynomials (pt(y)∈𝕂[y]:t=0,…,T)∈ASC(Y,T)(p_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]:t=0,\ldots,T)\in ASC(Y,T). We also denote by A​P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y) the class of all algebraic polynomial Stein operators for the target random variable YY.

Proposition 3.2.

Fix d≥1d\geq 1. Assume that the target random variable YY has the Gaussian polynomial form given by relation (3.1). Then, the following statements are in order:

  • (a)

    A​P​S​O​(Y)⊆P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y)\subseteq PSO(Y).

  • (b)

    When d=1d=1, we have A​P​S​O​(Y)=P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y)=PSO(Y) (or equivalently A​S​C​(Y,T)=S​C​(Y,T)ASC(Y,T)=SC(Y,T) for every T≥1T\geq 1).

Proof.

(a) Obvious. (b) Let 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈PSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in PSO(Y). Then by definition,

I​E​[gT​(X)+pT​(Y)|Y]=I​E​[gT​(X)+pT​(h⁡(X))|h⁡(X)]=0.{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[g_{T}(X)+p_{T}(Y)\,\big|\,Y\right]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\left[g_{T}(X)+p_{T}(h(X))\,\big|\,h(X)\right]=0.

Then, Lemma B.1 implies that either gT​(X)+pT​(h⁡(X))=0g_{T}(X)+p_{T}(h(X))=0 (that means 𝒮∈A​P​S​O​(Y)\mathcal{S}\in APSO(Y), and so nothing left to prove) or h⁡(X)h(X) is an even polynomial and gT​(X)+pT​(h⁡(X))g_{T}(X)+p_{T}(h(X)) is an odd polynomial. Next, first note that for hh being even, and any polynomial p∈𝕂⁡[X]p\in\mathbb{K}[X], the composition polynomial p⁡(h⁡(X))p(h(X)) is even. Next, we show that gT​(X)=∑t=0T−1ΓYT−t​pt​(h⁡(X))g_{T}(X)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Gamma^{T-t}_{Y}p_{t}(h(X)) is an even polynomial too. Note that, linearity of the ΓY\Gamma_{Y} operator allows us to write

∑t=0T−1ΓYT−t​pt​(h⁡(X))=ΓY​(∑t=1TΓYT−t​(pt−1​(h⁡(X)))).\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Gamma^{T-t}_{Y}p_{t}(h(X))=\Gamma_{Y}\Big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Gamma_{Y}^{T-t}\left(p_{t-1}(h(X))\right)\Big). (3.3)

Next, by definition of the ΓY\Gamma_{Y} operator we can write ΓY​(g⁡(X))=h′​(X)​δ−1​g​(X)\Gamma_{Y}(g(X))=h^{\prime}(X)\delta^{-1}g(X) for every given polynomial g∈𝕂⁡[X]g\in\mathbb{K}[X]. Hence, the ΓY\Gamma_{Y} operator maps an even polynomial g⁡(X)g(X) to a product of two odd polynomials, and ΓY​(g​(X))\Gamma_{Y}(g(X)) is also even since h⁡(X)h(X) is an even polynomial. The above reasoning yields that the polynomial argument inside the ΓY\Gamma_{Y} operator in the right hand side (3.3), which is given by

r⁡(X):=pT−1​(h⁡(X))+…+ΓYT−1​(p0​(h⁡(X))),r(X):=p_{T-1}(h(X))+\ldots+\Gamma^{T-1}_{Y}(p_{0}(h(X))),

is even, and ΓY​(r​(X))\Gamma_{Y}(r(X)) is even as well. Therefore, the polynomial gT​(X)+pT​(h⁡(X))g_{T}(X)+p_{T}(h(X)), being both even and odd, is necessarily zero, i.e. 𝒮∈A​P​S​O​(Y)\mathcal{S}\in APSO(Y). ∎

Corollary 3.1.

Let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1), and Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) so that h∈𝕂⁡[X]h\in\mathbb{K}[X] with deg⁡h≥2\deg{h}\geq 2 and I​E​[h⁡(X)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[h(X)]=0. Assume 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈PSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in PSO(Y) is a polynomial Stein operator for the target YY. Identify 𝕂⁡[y]≅𝕂⁡[h⁡(x)]\mathbb{K}[y]\cong\mathbb{K}[h(x)]. Then necessarily, pT​(y)∈𝕂⁡[y]∩⟨h′​(x)⟩p_{T}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]\cap\langle h^{\prime}(x)\rangle.

Proof.

Proposition 3.2, item (b) implies that 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈APSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in APSO(Y). Hence gT​(X)+pT​(h⁡(X))=0g_{T}(X)+p_{T}(h(X))=0. On the other hand, note that

pT​(h​(X))\displaystyle p_{T}(h(X)) =−(ΓYT​(p0)+…+ΓY​(pT−1))=−ΓY​(ΓYT−1​(p0)+…+pT−1​(X))\displaystyle=-\Big(\Gamma^{T}_{Y}(p_{0})+\ldots+\Gamma_{Y}(p_{T-1})\Big)=-\Gamma_{Y}\Big(\Gamma^{T-1}_{Y}(p_{0})+\ldots+p_{T-1}(X)\Big)
=−(D​Y,δ−1​(ΓYT−1​(p0)+…+pT−1​(X)))\displaystyle=-\Big(DY,\delta^{-1}\left(\Gamma^{T-1}_{Y}(p_{0})+\ldots+p_{T-1}(X)\right)\Big)
=−h′​(X)​δ−1​(ΓYT−1​(p0)+…+pT−1​(X))∈⟨h′​(X)⟩.\displaystyle=-h^{\prime}(X)\delta^{-1}\left(\Gamma^{T-1}_{Y}(p_{0})+\ldots+p_{T-1}(X)\right)\in\langle h^{\prime}(X)\rangle.

∎

Remark 3.2.
  • (i)

    In several important settings (such as when d=1d=1) algebraic polynomial Stein operators, when they exist, are easier to find compared to general polynomial Stein operators. This is due to the fact that one can settle the problem of finding an algebraic polynomial Stein operator in a completely algebraic framework – using the algebraic operators that are introduced in Section 2 – to bypass the difficult problem of computing the conditional expectation in the last stage of the general Stein chain. In fact, hereafter, this is our major interest that at last successfully leads to many new polynomial Stein operators for Gaussian polynomial targets of very complex probabilistic nature, whose derivation is far beyond available techniques from the literature.

  • (ii)

    For a Gaussian polynomial target random variable YY of the form (3.1), Proposition 3.2, item (b), implies that A​P​S​O​(Y)=P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y)=PSO(Y) when d=1d=1. However, in general,

    A​P​S​O​(Y)≠P​S​O​(Y), when d≥2.APSO(Y)\neq PSO(Y),\quad\text{ when }\quad d\geq 2. (3.4)

    This phenomenon is discussed in the forthcoming example, in which the significant role of probability enters through the conditional expectation. As will become clear, in higher dimensions, with the target random variable YY of the form (3.1), the situation I​E​[g⁡(X1,…,Xd)|Y]=p⁡(Y){\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\,|\,Y]=p(Y) most often happens for some polynomial p∈𝕂⁡[Y]p\in\mathbb{K}[Y], although g⁡(X1,…,Xd)∈𝕂⁡[X1,…,Xd]∖𝕂⁡[Y]g(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\in\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}]\setminus\mathbb{K}[Y]. Also, item (b) of the forthcoming example contains several examples of Gaussian polynomial target random variables Y=h⁡(X1,…,Xd)Y=h(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}) with d≥2d\geq 2 for which A​P​S​O​(Y)≠∅APSO(Y)\neq\emptyset.

Example 3.1.
  • (a)

    Case d=1d=1: Let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). Although Proposition 3.2, part (b), confirms that A​P​S​O​(Y)=P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y)=PSO(Y), we would like to present some concrete illustrative examples for some known polynomial Stein operators. (i) When Y=a​X+bY=aX+b, where a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}, it is clear that A​P​S​O​(Y)=P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y)=PSO(Y). (ii) Let Y=a​X2+b​X+cY=aX^{2}+bX+c, where a,b≠0a,b\neq 0 and a,b,c∈ℝa,b,c\in\mathbb{R}. Note that I​E​[Y]=a+c{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Y]=a+c. So, from the Malliavin–Stein perspective, the most desirerable choice for the zeroth polynomial is p0​(y)=y−a−cp_{0}(y)=y-a-c. Straightforward computations give that

    g1​(X)\displaystyle g_{1}(X) =ΓY​(p0​(Y))=ΓY​(Y−a−c)=ΓY​(Y)\displaystyle=\Gamma_{Y}(p_{0}(Y))=\Gamma_{Y}(Y-a-c)=\Gamma_{Y}(Y)
    =2​a2​H2​(X)+3​a​b​H1​(X)+(2​a2+b2),\displaystyle=2a^{2}H_{2}(X)+3abH_{1}(X)+(2a^{2}+b^{2}),

    and I​E​[g1​(X)]=2​a2+b2{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{1}(X)]=2a^{2}+b^{2}. The requirement a,b≠0a,b\neq 0 yields that g1​(X)≠p​(Y)g_{1}(X)\neq p(Y) almost surely for any polynomial p∈𝕂⁡[Y]p\in\mathbb{K}[Y]. Hence, we need to choose appropriately the next polynomial p1​(y)∈𝕂​[y]p_{1}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y] and move to the next stage. To do this, note that

    ΓY​(g1​(X))=4​a3​H2​(X)+8​a2​b​H1​(X)+(3​a​b2+4​a3).\displaystyle\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1}(X))=4a^{3}H_{2}(X)+8a^{2}bH_{1}(X)+(3ab^{2}+4a^{3}).

The polynomial p1​(y)=−4​a​(y−c)+(2​a2−b2)p_{1}(y)=-4a(y-c)+(2a^{2}-b^{2}) meets these requirements. It is easily checked that I​E​[g1​(X)]=−I​E​[p1​(Y)]{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{1}(X)]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{1}(Y)] and we also have that

    g2​(X)\displaystyle g_{2}(X) OPEN=ΓY​(g1​(X))+p1​(Y))=ΓY​(g1​(X)−4​a​ΓY​(Y)CLOSE\displaystyle=\Gamma_{Y}\left(g_{1}(X))+p_{1}(Y)\right)=\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1}(X)-4a\Gamma_{Y}(Y)
    =ΓY​(g1​(X))−4​a​ΓY​(p0​(Y))\displaystyle=\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1}(X))-4a\Gamma_{Y}(p_{0}(Y))
    =ΓY​(g1​(X))−4​a​g1​(X)\displaystyle=\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1}(X))-4ag_{1}(X)
    =−4​a3​H2​(X)−4​a2​b​H1​(X)−4​a3−a​b2\displaystyle=-4a^{3}H_{2}(X)-4a^{2}bH_{1}(X)-4a^{3}-ab^{2}
    =−4​a2​(Y−c)−a​b2.\displaystyle=-4a^{2}(Y-c)-ab^{2}.

    We now choose p2​(y)=4​a2​(y−c)+a​b2p_{2}(y)=4a^{2}(y-c)+ab^{2}, and note that g2+p2​(y)=0g_{2}+p_{2}(y)=0. Thus, the sequence (p0​(Y),p1​(Y),p2​(Y))(p_{0}(Y),p_{1}(Y),p_{2}(Y)) is an algebraic stein chain of length T=2T=2 for the target random variable YY. Finally, applying Proposition 3.1 yields the Stein operator

    𝒮=(ab2+4a2(y−c))∂2+(2a2−b2−4a(y−c))∂+(y−c−a),\mathcal{S}=\left(ab^{2}+4a^{2}(y-c)\right)\partial^{2}+\left(2a^{2}-b^{2}-4a(y-c)\right)\partial+(y-c-a),

    which was achieved in [28, Proposition 2.1] via a different approach.

  • (b)

    General Case: Let {Xk∼N⁡(0,1):k∈ℕ}\{X_{k}\sim N(0,1)\,:\,k\in\mathbb{N}\} be a family of i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables.

    (i) Consider the target random variables Y=∑k=1Kαk​H2​(X)Y=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_{k}H_{2}(X) (living in the second Wiener chaos) where the αk\alpha_{k} are non-zero real numbers. Note that by choosing αk=α\alpha_{k}=\alpha for k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, the random variable YY boils down to that of the centered gamma distribution with KK degrees of freedom, and by choosing αk=α,−β\alpha_{k}=\alpha,-\beta for k=1,…,rk=1,\ldots,r, and k=r+1,…,2​r(=K)k=r+1,\ldots,2r(=K), respectively, where α​β>0\alpha\beta>0, the random variable YY boils down to that of the centered variance-gamma distribution [25] with parameters (r,θ,σ)(r,\theta,\sigma), where θ=α−β\theta=\alpha-\beta and σ=2​α​β\sigma=2\sqrt{\alpha\beta}. In [3], the authors provided the following polynomial Stein operator of order TT with linear coefficients for the target random variable YY:

    𝒮=∑k=1T(bk−aky)∂k−a0y,\mathcal{S}=\sum_{k=1}^{T}(b_{k}-a_{k}y)\partial^{k}-a_{0}y, (3.5)

    where the constants (ak,bk:k=0,…,T)(a_{k},b_{k}:k=0,\ldots,T) are explicit and given in [3, Section 2.1], and TT is the number of distinct coefficients in (αk,k=1,…,K)(\alpha_{k},\,k=1,\ldots,K). Next, relying on [9, Lemma 3], relation (23), we can easily infer that 𝒮∈A​P​S​O​(Y)\mathcal{S}\in APSO(Y) is an algebraic polynomial Stein operator for YY. Up to now, only when K=1K=1 (equivalently d=1d=1, and corresponding to a scaled centered gamma random variable) do we know that A​P​S​O​(Y)=P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y)=PSO(Y). For example, with the product Gaussian distribution Y=X1​X2Y=X_{1}X_{2} we do not know whether A​P​S​O​(Y)=P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y)=PSO(Y).

    (ii) The following example provides a polynomial Stein operator that is not algebraic with d=2d=2. Consider the target Y=X12​X22Y=X^{2}_{1}X^{2}_{2}, a product of two independent chi-square random variables, each with one degree of freedom. In [27], the author provided the following second order polynomial Stein operator

    𝒮=y2∂2+2y∂+14(1−y).\mathcal{S}=y^{2}\partial^{2}+2y\partial+\frac{1}{4}(1-y). (3.6)

    Using some straightforward computations, one can see that

    g1​(X1,X2)=ΓY​(p0​(Y))=−14​ΓY​(Y)=−Y4​(H2​(X1)+H2​(X2)+4)∈𝕂⁡[X1,X2].g_{1}(X_{1},X_{2})=\Gamma_{Y}(p_{0}(Y))=-\frac{1}{4}\Gamma_{Y}(Y)=-\frac{Y}{4}\biggl(H_{2}(X_{1})+H_{2}(X_{2})+4\biggr)\in\mathbb{K}[X_{1},X_{2}].

This yields that g2​(X1,X2)+p2​(Y)=g2​(X1,X2)+Y2≠0g_{2}(X_{1},X_{2})+p_{2}(Y)=g_{2}(X_{1},X_{2})+Y^{2}\neq 0 almost surely, and hence, 𝒮∉A​P​S​O​(Y)\mathcal{S}\notin APSO(Y) is not an algebraic polynomial Stein operator for the target YY. It is an interesting problem to determine whether A​P​S​O​(Y)≠∅APSO(Y)\neq\emptyset.

    (iii) The following example provides a polynomial Stein operator that is not algebraic with d=3d=3. Let Y=X1​X2​X3Y=X_{1}X_{2}X_{3} be the product of three independent standard Gaussian random variables. In [26], the author provides the following third order polynomial Stein operator for the target random variable YY:

    𝒮=y2∂3+3y∂2+∂−y∈PSO(Y).\mathcal{S}=y^{2}\partial^{3}+3y\partial^{2}+\partial-y\in PSO(Y).

    Some tedious computations yield that

    g1​(X1,X2,X3)\displaystyle g_{1}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}) =−ΓY​(Y)\displaystyle=-\Gamma_{Y}(Y)
    =−13​(H2​(X2)​H2​(X3)+H2​(X2)+H2​(X3)+1)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{3}\Big(H_{2}(X_{2})H_{2}(X_{3})+H_{2}(X_{2})+H_{2}(X_{3})+1\Big)
    −13​(H2​(X1)​H2​(X3)+H2​(X1)+H2​(X3)+1)\displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{3}\Big(H_{2}(X_{1})H_{2}(X_{3})+H_{2}(X_{1})+H_{2}(X_{3})+1\Big)
