    g2​(X1,X2,X3)\displaystyle g_{2}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}) =−ΓY​(g1+p1)=−ΓY​(g1+1)=−ΓY​(g1)\displaystyle=-\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1}+p_{1})=-\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1}+1)=-\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1})
    =−13​Y​(H2​(X1)+H2​(X2)+H2​(X3))−2​Y∈𝕂⁡[X1,X2,X3],\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{3}Y\Big(H_{2}(X_{1})+H_{2}(X_{2})+H_{2}(X_{3})\Big)-2Y\in\mathbb{K}[X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}],

    and

    ΓY​(g2​(X1,X2,X3))\displaystyle\Gamma_{Y}(g_{2}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})) =−ΓY​(ΓY​(g1))\displaystyle=-\Gamma_{Y}\left(\Gamma_{Y}(g_{1})\right)
    =−115​(H2​(X1)​X22​X32+13​H3​(X1)​X1​X32+13​X1​H3​(X1)​X22)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{15}\Big(H_{2}(X_{1})X^{2}_{2}X^{2}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}H_{3}(X_{1})X_{1}X^{2}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}X_{1}H_{3}(X_{1})X^{2}_{2}\Big)
    −115​(H2​(X2)​X12​X32+13​H3​(X2)​X2​X32+13​X12​X2​H3​(X3))\displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{15}\Big(H_{2}(X_{2})X^{2}_{1}X^{2}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}H_{3}(X_{2})X_{2}X^{2}_{3}+\frac{1}{3}X^{2}_{1}X_{2}H_{3}(X_{3})\Big)
    −115​(X12​X22​H2​(X3)+13​X12​X3​H3​(X3)+13​X22​X3​H3​(X3))\displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{15}\Big(X^{2}_{1}X^{2}_{2}H_{2}(X_{3})+\frac{1}{3}X^{2}_{1}X_{3}H_{3}(X_{3})+\frac{1}{3}X^{2}_{2}X_{3}H_{3}(X_{3})\Big)
    −14​g1​(X1,X2,X3)∈𝕂⁡[X1,X2,X3].\displaystyle\quad-\frac{1}{4}g_{1}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})\in\mathbb{K}[X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}].

    Hence, g3​(X1,X2,X3)+p3​(Y)=ΓY​(g2​(X1,X2,X3))−3​g1​(X1,X2,X3)+Y2≠0g_{3}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})+p_{3}(Y)=\Gamma_{Y}(g_{2}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}))-3g_{1}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})+Y^{2}\neq 0 almost surely, whilst I​E​[g3​(X1,X2,X3)+p3​(Y)|Y]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{3}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})+p_{3}(Y)\,|\,Y]=0 almost surely. In contrast to the product of two independent standard Gaussian random variables, we do not know yet whether the product of three or more independent standard Gaussian random variables admit any algebraic polynomial Stein operator.

Remark 3.3.
  1. (i)

    The following algorithm can be used to produce the associated algebraic Stein chains:

     

    Algorithm : Producing forward algebraic Stein chain

     
    1. (a)

      At stage t=0t=0, pick a polynomial p0∈𝕂⁡[Y]p_{0}\in\mathbb{K}[Y] such that I​E​[p0​(Y)]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(Y)]=0, and set g0=−I​E​[p0​(Y)]=0g_{0}=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(Y)]=0,

    2. (b)

      At stage t>1t>1, with chosen polynomials (p0,p1,…,pt−1)(p_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{t-1}) in the subring 𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{K}[Y] satisfying moment property I​E​[ps​(Y)]=−I​E​[gs]{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{s}(Y)]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{s}] for s=0,…,t−1s=0,\ldots,t-1, if

      gt:=ΓY​(gt−1+pt−1​(Y))∈𝕂⁡[Y]\displaystyle g_{t}:=\Gamma_{Y}\bigl(g_{t-1}+p_{t-1}(Y)\bigr)\in\mathbb{K}[Y]

      set pt​(Y)=−gtp_{t}(Y)=-g_{t} and stop.

    3. (c)

      Otherwise, choose a polynomial pt​(Y)∈𝕂​[Y]p_{t}(Y)\in\mathbb{K}[Y] with I​E​[pt​(Y)]=−I​E​[gt]{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{t}(Y)]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[g_{t}], and continue to stage (t+1)(t+1).

     
  2. (ii)

    We have not yet explained how to choose the polynomials pt​(Y)p_{t}(Y) and how to determine whether algebraic Stein chains of finite length beginning with initial state p0​(Y)p_{0}(Y) do exist. This is in fact the topic of Section 3.3. The question of how to chose the initial state is also of interest. In the Malliavin-Stein method, it is often desirable to take p0​(y)=c​yp_{0}(y)=cy as the zeroth-order term; however, other choices of initial state can lead to Stein operators with smaller degree mm or smaller order TT (see Table 1). Remark C.1 describes how initial states can be chosen to obtain such Stein operators.

  3. (iii)

    Instead of looking for polynomial coefficients in 𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{K}[Y], we could restrict the coefficients to be in a linear subspace, as for example

    𝕃=𝕂r​[Y]={p⁡(Y): polynomials with ​deg⁡(p)≤r}.\displaystyle\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{K}_{r}[Y]=\bigl\{p(Y)\,:\,\text{ polynomials with }\deg{(p)}\leq r\bigr\}.

    This observation is vital for our final goal of finding an algebraic Stein chain by implementing a MATLAB code (see Remark 3.7, item (ii)). We could also formulate the problem with a sequence of possibly different subspaces 𝕃t⊆𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{L}_{t}\subseteq\mathbb{K}[Y] at each stage t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}. Note also that if

    ⟨∇h​(X1,…,Xd)⟩∩𝕂r​[Y]={0},\displaystyle\big\langle\nabla h(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})\big\rangle\cap\mathbb{K}_{r}[Y]=\{0\},

    there cannot be any non-trivial finite order algebraic polynomial Stein operator satisfying deg⁡pt​(y)≤r,\deg p_{t}(y)\leq r, ∀t\forall t.

3.2 Backward Stein chain

We may also validate an algebraic Stein chain by starting from the highest order term and checking recursively the lower order terms. We illustrate this subsidiary approach only in the univariate case d=1d=1 (see Remark 3.4 for the multidimensional case). We start from the highest order derivative coefficient pT​(Y)∈⟨∂h⁡(X)⟩∩𝕂⁡[Y]p_{T}(Y)\in\langle\partial h(X)\rangle\cap\mathbb{K}[Y] (if this condition is not satisfied, we stop with a negative answer: there cannot be an algebraic polynomial Stein operator with highest order coefficient pT​(Y)p_{T}(Y)). Let

qT(X)=−pT(h(X))/∂h(X).q_{T}(X)=-p_{T}(h(X))/\partial h(X). (3.7)

After tt successful recursion steps, we should have

δ​qT−t​(X)∈(⟨∂h⁡(X)⟩+𝕂⁡[Y]).\displaystyle\delta q_{T-t}(X)\in\left(\Big\langle\partial h(X)\Big\rangle+\mathbb{K}[Y]\right). (3.8)

If this condition is not satisfied we stop with a negative answer; otherwise, there is a polynomial of the target pT−t−1​(Y)p_{T-t-1}(Y) such that (δ​qT−t​(X)−pT−t−1​(h⁡(X)))∈⟨∂h⁡(X)⟩\bigl(\delta q_{T-t}(X)-p_{T-t-1}(h(X))\bigr)\in\langle\partial h(X)\rangle. We set

qT−t−1​(X)=(δ​qT−t​(X)−pT−t−1​(h⁡(X)))/∂h⁡(X)\displaystyle q_{T-t-1}(X)=\bigl(\delta q_{T-t}(X)-p_{T-t-1}(h(X))\bigr)/\partial h(X)

and continue. The algebraic backward Stein chain ends successfully after (T−1)(T-1) backward steps when

δ​qT​(X)=p0​(h⁡(X))=p0​(Y)∈𝕂⁡[Y].\displaystyle\delta q_{T}(X)=p_{0}(h(X))=p_{0}(Y)\in\mathbb{K}[Y].

In such case

I​E​[p0​(Y)​f​(Y)]=I​E​[δ⁡(q1​(X))​f​(Y)]=I​E​[q1​(X)​∂h⁡(X)​∂f⁡(Y)]\displaystyle{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[p_{0}(Y)f(Y)\bigr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[\delta(q_{1}(X))f(Y)\bigr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[q_{1}(X)\partial h(X)\partial f(Y)\bigr]
=I​E​[δ​q2​(X)−p1​(Y)∂h⁡(X)​∂h⁡(X)​∂f⁡(Y)]=−I​E​[p1​(Y)​∂f⁡(Y)]+I​E​[δ​q2​(X)​∂f⁡(Y)]=…\displaystyle={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\biggl[\frac{\delta q_{2}(X)-p_{1}(Y)}{\partial h(X)}\partial h(X)\partial f(Y)\biggr]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[p_{1}(Y)\partial f(Y)\bigr]+{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[\delta q_{2}(X)\partial f(Y)\bigr]=\dots
=−I​E​[p1​(Y)​∂f⁡(Y)]−I​E​[p2​(Y)​∂2f⁡(Y)]−⋯−I​E​[pT−1​(Y)​∂T−1f⁡(Y)]\displaystyle=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[p_{1}(Y)\partial f(Y)\bigr]-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[p_{2}(Y)\partial^{2}f(Y)\bigr]-\dots-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[p_{T-1}(Y)\partial^{T-1}f(Y)\bigr]
+I​E​[δ​qT​(X)​∂T−1f⁡(Y)],\displaystyle\quad+{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[\delta q_{T}(X)\partial^{T-1}f(Y)\bigr],

with

I​E​[δ​qT​(X)​∂T−1f⁡(Y)]=I​E​[qT​(X)​∂h⁡(Y)​∂Tf⁡(Y)]=−I​E​[pT​(Y)​∂Tf⁡(Y)],\displaystyle{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[\delta q_{T}(X)\partial^{T-1}f(Y)\bigr]={\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[q_{T}(X)\partial h(Y)\partial^{T}f(Y)\bigr]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{T}(Y)\partial^{T}f(Y)\bigr],

which means that 𝒮​f​(y)=∑t=0Tpt​(y)​∂tf⁡(y){\mathcal{S}}f(y)=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}(y)\partial^{t}f(y) is an algebraic polynomial Stein operator for the target Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X).

Remark 3.4.

In this remark X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}). The backward construction of an algebraic Stein chain in the multidimensional case (d>1)(d>1) is essentially the same as in the univariate case d=1d=1 with only the minor difference that at each backward step the divisor polynomials qT−t,t=0,…,T−1q_{T-t},\,t=0,\ldots,T-1, are not unique, unlike the univariate case. For example, start with the polynomial coefficient pT​(Y)p_{T}(Y) of the highest order term that must be in 𝕂⁡[Y]∩⟨D​h​(X)⟩\mathbb{K}[Y]\cap\langle Dh(X)\rangle. (If this condition is not valid, we know there is no algebraic polynomial Stein operator with the highest order coefficient term pTp_{T}. This condition can be checked by the multivariate polynomial division algorithm, using Gröbner basis.) The latter means there is some polynomial vector qT​(X)=(qT,1​(X),…,qT,d​(X))∈𝕂​[X]dq_{T}(X)=(q_{T,1}(X),\dots,q_{T,d}(X))\in\mathbb{K}[X]^{d} such that

pT​(h⁡(X))=∑k=1dqT,k​(X)​Dk​h​(X).\displaystyle p_{T}(h(X))=\sum_{k=1}^{d}q_{T,k}(X)D_{k}h(X).

However, when the condition is satisfied, (when d>1d>1) the divisor polynomial qT​(X)q_{T}(X) does not need to be unique. In fact, one can add any solution of the homogeneous equation

∑k=1duT,k​(X)​Dk​h​(X)=0.\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{d}u_{T,k}(X)D_{k}h(X)=0.

This point has to be compared with relation (3.7) in the univariate case d=1d=1 where the divisor polynomial qTq_{T} is unique.

3.3 Null controllability

This section outlines the connection between Stein’s method and the theory of linear systems. For a comprehensive account of the theory of linear systems, the reader is referred to [57, 23, 24, 13, 14] and references therein. Let 𝕍\mathbb{V} (state space) and 𝕃\mathbb{L} (control space) be two vector spaces (not necessarily finite dimensional) over 𝕂\mathbb{K}. A linear discrete system Σ\Sigma is a quadruple (𝕍,𝕃,Γ,Λ)(\mathbb{V},\mathbb{L},\Gamma,\Lambda), where Γ:𝕍→𝕍\Gamma:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{V} (evolution operator) and Λ:𝕃→𝕍\Lambda:\mathbb{L}\to\mathbb{V} (input operator) are two linear maps, and the state variables follow the following linear dynamic

gt=Γgt−1+Λpt−1,t=1,2,….\displaystyle g_{t}=\Gamma g_{t-1}+\Lambda p_{t-1},\quad t=1,2,\ldots. (3.9)

Let us introduce the notion of (null) controllability in the theory of linear systems, another component that plays a significant role in our paper.

Definition 3.3.

Let T≥1T\geq 1. We say that an initial state g0∈𝕍g_{0}\in\mathbb{V} is null controllable in TT-steps and denoted by g1  ↝T Σ 0g_{1}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.00002pt\hskip-5.00002pt\hbox{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\rightsquigarrow$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.51479pt\raisebox{4.77881pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle T$}}\hskip-2.51479pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\hskip-5.00002pt\hskip-2.39586pt\raisebox{-4.3988pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma$}}\hskip-2.39586pt\hskip 5.00002pt}}0, if there is a finite (null) control sequence {p0,…,pT−1}⊆𝕃\{p_{0},\dots,p_{T-1}\}\subseteq\mathbb{L} such that the linear recursion (3.9) reaches gT=0∈𝕍g_{T}=0\in\mathbb{V} at time TT. Denote

𝒩⁡(Σ,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\Sigma,T) ={g0∈𝕍:g0  ↝T Σ 0}.\displaystyle=\left\{g_{0}\in\mathbb{V}\,:\,g_{0}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.00002pt\hskip-5.00002pt\hbox{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\rightsquigarrow$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-2.51479pt\raisebox{4.77881pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle T$}}\hskip-2.51479pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\hskip-5.00002pt\hskip-2.39586pt\raisebox{-4.3988pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\Sigma$}}\hskip-2.39586pt\hskip 5.00002pt}}0\right\}.

The set of all null controllable states is 𝒞⁡(Σ)=⋃T≥1𝒞⁡(Σ,T)\mathscr{C}(\Sigma)=\bigcup_{T\geq 1}\mathscr{C}(\Sigma,T). Clearly, both 𝒞⁡(Σ,T)\mathscr{C}(\Sigma,T) and 𝒞⁡(Σ)\mathscr{C}(\Sigma) are vector spaces over 𝕂\mathbb{K}, and 𝒞⁡(Σ,T)⊆𝒞⁡(Σ,T+1)\mathscr{C}(\Sigma,T)\subseteq\mathscr{C}(\Sigma,T+1) for every T≥1T\geq 1.

Lemma 3.1.

Consider a linear discrete system Σ\Sigma as described above. Then, the state g0∈𝕍g_{0}\in\mathbb{V} is null controllable if and only if for some T≥1T\geq 1,

ΓT​g0∈∑t=1TΓT−t​Λ​(𝕃).\Gamma^{T}g_{0}\in\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Gamma^{T-t}\Lambda(\mathbb{L}).
Proof.

Using the linear dynamic (3.9) one can readily obtain that, for t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T,

gt=Γt​g0+∑s=1tΓt−s​Λ​ps−1,\displaystyle g_{t}=\Gamma^{t}g_{0}+\sum_{s=1}^{t}\Gamma^{t-s}\Lambda p_{s-1},

and hence, the result follows at once.∎

Remark 3.5.

  1. If the null controllability problem has finite horizon solutions the following algorithm finds the shortest null control sequences:

     

    Algorithm : Finding null control sequence

     
    • (a)

      At stage t=0t=0, pick an initial state g0∈𝕍g_{0}\in\mathbb{V}, and consider the linear equation

      Γ​g0=−Λ​p0.\displaystyle\Gamma g_{0}=-\Lambda p_{0}.

      If this equation has a solution in 𝕃\mathbb{L}, then stop (equivalently, Γ⁡(−g0)∈Range​(Λ)\Gamma(-g_{0})\in\text{Range}(\Lambda)).

    • (b)

      Otherwise we continue the recursion, until at some stage TT for the first time the system

      ΓT​g0=−(Λ​pT−1+Γ​Λ​pT−2+Γ2​pT−3+⋯+ΓT−2​Λ​p1+ΓT−1​Λ​p0)\displaystyle\Gamma^{T}g_{0}=-\bigl(\Lambda p_{T-1}+\Gamma\Lambda p_{T-2}+\Gamma^{2}p_{T-3}+\dots+\Gamma^{T-2}\Lambda p_{1}+\Gamma^{T-1}\Lambda p_{0}\bigr) (3.10)

      has solution (which is not necessarily unique) (p0,…,pT−1)∈𝕃T(p_{0},\dots,p_{T-1})\in\mathbb{L}^{T}.

     

The linear control framework applies directly to our forward algebraic Stein chain construction. To see this, consider the linear system Σ\Sigma, where the state space 𝕍=𝕂⁡[X1,…,Xd]\mathbb{V}=\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\dots,X_{d}] and the control space 𝕃=𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{K}[Y]. We stress that both the state and control spaces are infinite dimensional vector spaces which do not enjoy suitable analytic properties such as being a Banach space. Moreover, the evolution and input operators are given by the Malliavin operator (X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})),

ΓY:𝕂⁡[X1,…,Xd]→⟨∂X1h⁡(X),…,∂Xdh⁡(X)⟩⊆𝕂⁡[X1,…,Xd].\displaystyle\Gamma_{Y}:\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\dots,X_{d}]\to\Big\langle\partial_{X_{1}}h(X),\ldots,\partial_{X_{d}}h(X)\Big\rangle\subseteq\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\dots,X_{d}].

The following result is an immediate consequence of the definitions of an algebraic Stein chain and a null controllable state.

Proposition 3.3.

Fix T≥1T\geq 1. Let d≥1d\geq 1, and assume that the Gaussian polynomial target variable YY takes the form (3.1). Let Σ=(𝕍,𝕃,ΓY,ΓY)\Sigma=(\mathbb{V},\mathbb{L},\Gamma_{Y},\Gamma_{Y}) be the linear system as described above. Let

𝕂0​[Y]={p⁡(Y)∈𝕂⁡[Y]:I​E​[p⁡(Y)]=0}.\mathbb{K}_{0}[Y]=\Big\{p(Y)\in\mathbb{K}[Y]\,:\,{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p(Y)]=0\Big\}. (3.11)
  • (a)

    Then, there is a surjective binary relation (and not a function) between the set 𝒞⁡(Σ,T)∩𝕂0​[Y]\mathscr{C}(\Sigma,T)\cap\mathbb{K}_{0}[Y] and the set A​S​C​(Y,T)ASC(Y,T) of all algebraic Stein chains of length TT. Moreover, there is a surjective binary relation between the set 𝒞​(Σ)∩𝕂0​[Y]\mathscr{C}(\Sigma)\cap\mathbb{K}_{0}[Y] and the set A​P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y) of all the algebraic polynomial Stein operators for the target random variable YY.

  • (b)

    When d=1d=1, the same statement as in item (a) holds by replacing everywhere A​S​C​(Y,T)ASC(Y,T) with S​C​(Y,T)SC(Y,T), and A​P​S​O​(Y)APSO(Y) with P​S​O​(Y)PSO(Y), respectively.

Proof.

(a) For a given g0∈𝒞⁡(Σ,T)∩𝕂0​[Y]g_{0}\in\mathscr{C}(\Sigma,T)\cap\mathbb{K}_{0}[Y], and p=(pt(y)∈𝕂[y]:t=0,…,T−1)∈ASC(Y,T)p=(p_{t}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]\,:\,t=0,\ldots,T-1)\in ASC(Y,T), we say that g0​R​pg_{0}Rp if the sequence pp is a null control sequence for g0g_{0}. Clearly, RR defines a surjective (but not injective) relation that is not a function, since in general null control sequences (even of the same length) are not unique. The other statement follows directly from Propositions 3.1, and 3.2. (b) Apply Proposition 3.2, item (b). ∎

Remark 3.6.

Assume the convention X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}) as above. Let p0∈𝕃=𝕂⁡[Y]p_{0}\in\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{K}[Y]. Then, the target random variable Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) admits an algebraic polynomial Stein operator with zeroth order term p0p_{0} if the initial state g0=g0​(X):=ΓY​p0​(h⁡(X))g_{0}=g_{0}(X):=\Gamma_{Y}p_{0}(h(X)) can be null controllable in a finite time. Mathematically, for some t≥1t\geq 1, there exist polynomials p0​(Y),…,pt−1​(Y)∈𝕂⁡[Y]p_{0}(Y),\dots,p_{t-1}(Y)\in\mathbb{K}[Y] such that

gt+1​(X)=Γt​g0​(X)+∑s=1tΓYt−s​ps−1​(h⁡(X))=0.\displaystyle g_{t+1}(X)=\Gamma^{t}g_{0}(X)+\sum_{s=1}^{t}\Gamma_{Y}^{t-s}p_{s-1}(h(X))=0. (3.12)

The latter is a direct consequence of the set inclusion ΓYt​(𝕂⁡[Y])⊆∑s=1tΓYt−s​(𝕂⁡[Y])\Gamma^{t}_{Y}(\mathbb{K}[Y])\subseteq\sum_{s=1}^{t}\Gamma^{t-s}_{Y}(\mathbb{K}[Y]) which is in order as soon as the ascending chain I1⊆⋯⊆It⊆It+1⊆⋯I_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq I_{t}\subseteq I_{t+1}\subseteq\cdots would stop, where It=∑s=1tΓYt−s​(𝕂⁡[Y])I_{t}=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\Gamma^{t-s}_{Y}(\mathbb{K}[Y]) for t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}. Although, the Hilbert base theorem guarantees that 𝕂⁡[X]\mathbb{K}[X] is a Noetherin ring, however we cannot conclude that the chain would necessary stop due to the undesirable fact that the vector spaces ItI_{t} are not ideal.

Remark 3.7.
  • (i)

    In order to apply the rich theory of linear control systems in our framework, we mention the following issues. Firstly, in our formulation, both the state and the control spaces are infinite dimensional vector spaces over 𝕂\mathbb{K}. Secondly, it is also possible that one can think of the (infinite dimensional) Hilbert state space 𝕍=L2​(μ)\mathbb{V}=L^{2}(\mu) with μ\mu the standard Gaussian measure on the real line. However, the control space 𝕃\mathbb{L} “must" be taken as the ring 𝕂⁡[Y]\mathbb{K}[Y], which is not a Hilbert space (not even a Banach space). Therefore, we believe that the theory developed for infinite dimensional linear systems, see for instance [23, 62, 63], is hardly applicable in our setting to study the null controllability.

  • (ii)

    To bypass the obstacles mentioned above, in the computer implementation of the algorithm we may set an upper bound on the polynomial degree of the Stein operator coefficients, assuming that the initial state and controls belong to 𝕃=𝕂m​[Y]\mathbb{L}=\mathbb{K}_{m}[Y]. Then, at stage tt,

    deg(gt)≤{deg⁡(h)×m+(deg⁡(h)−2)×t(univariate h)deg⁡(h)×(m+t) (multivariate h).\displaystyle\deg(g_{t})\leq\left\{\begin{matrix}\deg(h)\times m+(\deg(h)-2)\times t&\mbox{(univariate $h$)}\\ \deg(h)\times(m+t)&\mbox{ (multivariate $h$).}\end{matrix}\right.

    Hence, in our linear system, state space is time varying (increasing in time); however, within a finite time horizon TT we can implement the algorithm to check null controllability up to time TT on a finite dimensional state space ℝdeg⁡(h)×m+(deg⁡(h)−2)×T\mathbb{R}^{\deg(h)\times m+(\deg(h)-2)\times T} and control space ℝdeg⁡(h)×m\mathbb{R}^{\deg(h)\times m}, see also Remark 3.3. Moreover, we point out that even by fixing a time horizon TT, the Kalman criterion as described in the introduction) cannot be used to study null controllability, because the criterion checks null controllability within the whole null states 𝒞⁡(Σ)\mathscr{C}(\Sigma) and not on 𝒞⁡(Σ,T)\mathscr{C}(\Sigma,T). Lastly, in the computer implementation of the linear system Σ\Sigma (as described above) the input operator Λ=ΓY​Θ\Lambda=\Gamma_{Y}\Theta, where the operator Θ\Theta is given by the embedding p⁡(Y)∈𝕂⁡[Y]p(Y)\in\mathbb{K}[Y] into p⁡(h⁡(X1,…,Xd))∈𝕂⁡[X1,…,Xd]p(h(X_{1},\dots,X_{d}))\in\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\dots,X_{d}]. This is due to the fact that operator δ−1\delta^{-1} (in the definition of the ΓY\Gamma_{Y} operator) acts over the polynomial ring 𝕂⁡[X1,…,Xd]\mathbb{K}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}].

Remark 3.8.

In the Malliavin-Stein method, the zeroth-order polynomial p0​(y)=c​yp_{0}(y)=cy is commonly used. However, other choices of p0​(y)p_{0}(y) may allow for Stein operators with either lower order TT or lower maximal coefficient degree mm. In the computer implementation of our algorithm, for a given target Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) the input is a zeroth-order polynomial coefficient p0​(h​(x))p_{0}(h(x)), with I​E​[p0​(h⁡(X))]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(h(X))]=0. In order to find a Stein operator with generic p0​(y)p_{0}(y) we run the algorithm several times with the respective initial coefficients p0(k)​(y)=yk−I​E​[h​(X)k]p_{0}^{(k)}(y)=y^{k}-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[h(X)^{k}], in order to obtain the corresponding Stein operators satisfying

I​E​[𝒮(k)​f​(Y)]=−I​E​[p0​(Y)​f​(Y)]\displaystyle{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[{\mathcal{S}}^{(k)}f(Y)\bigr]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[p_{0}(Y)f(Y)\bigr]

for k=1,…,m0k=1,\dots,m_{0}. When the Stein chains end successfully and Stein operators are found for the initial coefficients above, by solving a linear system for the linear combination one can further reduce the order or the maximal coefficient degree of a Stein operator with a generic zeroth-order polynomial coefficient p0​(y)p_{0}(y) of degree ≤m0\leq m_{0}.

4 Applications to Gaussian Hermite polynomials

4.1 Highest order polynomial coefficient

Before the next proposition, we note the following lemma that will be needed in the proof. The result of [33] is stated for the physicists’ Hermite polynomials rather than the probabilists’ Hermite polynomials, as used in our paper.

Lemma 4.1.

([33]). Define Ep(x)=(π1/222​pp!)−1/2e−x2/4Hp(x)E_{p}(x)=(\pi^{1/2}2^{2p}p!)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/4}H_{p}(x). Then the relative maxima of |Ep​(x)||E_{p}(x)|, x≥0x\geq 0, steadily increase, i.e., if x1<x2<…<xjx_{1}<x_{2}<\ldots<x_{j} are the non-negative zeros of Ep′E_{p}^{\prime} for fixed pp, then

|Ep​(x1)|<|Ep​(x2)|<…<|Ep​(xj)|.|E_{p}(x_{1})|<|E_{p}(x_{2})|<\ldots<|E_{p}(x_{j})|.
Proposition 4.1.

Let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). Assume that Y=Hp​(X)Y=H_{p}(X), where HpH_{p} is the Hermite polynomial of degree p≥2p\geq 2 (the case p=1p=1 corresponds to standard Gaussian distribution that is not of interest in this paper). Let 𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t∈PSO(Y)=APSO(Y)\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}\in PSO(Y)=APSO(Y) be a polynomial Stein operator for YY. As before, identify the (dependent) variable y=Hp​(x)y=H_{p}(x). Then the following properties hold:

  1. (a)

    𝕂⁡[y]∩⟨Hp′​(x)⟩\mathbb{K}[y]\cap\langle H^{\prime}_{p}(x)\rangle is an ideal of the subring 𝕂⁡[y]\mathbb{K}[y]. Moreover,

    𝕂⁡[y]∩⟨Hp′​(x)⟩=⟨t⁡(y)⟩\displaystyle\mathbb{K}[y]\cap\langle H^{\prime}_{p}(x)\rangle=\langle t(y)\rangle

    with

    t(y)=∏z:Hp′​(z)=0(y−Hp(z)).\displaystyle t(y)=\prod_{z:H^{\prime}_{p}(z)=0}\bigl(y-H_{p}(z)\bigr).
  2. (b)

    pT​(y)∈𝕂⁡[y]∩⟨Hp′​(x)⟩p_{T}(y)\in\mathbb{K}[y]\cap\langle H^{\prime}_{p}(x)\rangle, and pT​(Hp​(x))=0p_{T}(H_{p}(x))=0 for all solutions xx of Hp′​(x)=0H^{\prime}_{p}(x)=0. In particular, pT​(y)=0p_{T}(y)=0 at all local minimum or local maximum values yy of HpH_{p}.

  3. (c)

    deg⁡(pT)≥p/2\mathrm{deg}(p_{T})\geq p/2 if pp is even, and deg⁡(pT)≥p−1\mathrm{deg}(p_{T})\geq p-1 if pp is odd.

Proof.

(a) It is easy to see that 𝕂⁡[y]∩⟨Hp′​(x)⟩⊆𝕂⁡[y]\mathbb{K}[y]\cap\langle H^{\prime}_{p}(x)\rangle\subseteq\mathbb{K}[y] is an ideal of the subring 𝕂⁡[y]\mathbb{K}[y]. Also, after substitution y=Hp​(x)y=H_{p}(x), it becomes clear that the polynomial t⁡(y)=t⁡(Hp​(x))t(y)=t(H_{p}(x)), given by t(y)=∏z:Hp′​(z)=0(y−Hp(z))∈𝕂[y],t(y)=\prod_{z:H^{\prime}_{p}(z)=0}\bigl(y-H_{p}(z)\bigr)\in\mathbb{K}[y], is divisible by Hp′​(x)H^{\prime}_{p}(x) by using the Taylor expansion Hp​(x)−Hp​(z)=∑k=1pHp(k)​(z)​(x−z)kH_{p}(x)-H_{p}(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{p}H^{(k)}_{p}(z)(x-z)^{k} for every zz such that Hp′​(z)=0H^{\prime}_{p}(z)=0. Note that Hp′​(x)=p​Hp−1​(x)H^{\prime}_{p}(x)=pH_{p-1}(x) and all the roots of the Hermite polynomials are real. So the claim follows at once by a direct application of Remark 2.1.

(b) Apply Corollary 3.1. The rest are direct consequences.

(c) This follows from part (b) and the fact that HpH_{p} has p/2p/2 distinct values for the local maxima and minima when pp is even, and p−1p-1 distinct values for the local maxima and minima when pp is odd. It is a standard property of HpH_{p} that it has exactly pp real roots. Therefore HpH_{p} must have pp local maxima and minima when pp is even and p−1p-1 local maxima and minima when pp is odd. But when pp is even, HpH_{p} is an even function and there can hence be at most p/2p/2 distinct values for the local maxima and minima. That there are exactly p/2p/2 distinct local maxima and minima in the even case now follows from the stronger result of Lemma 4.1. For odd pp, we let x1<x2<…<x(p−1)/2x_{1}<x_{2}<\ldots<x_{(p-1)/2} be the non-negative zeros of Hp′H_{p}^{\prime}, and as HpH_{p} is an odd function we have that −x(p−1)/2<…<−x2<−x1-x_{(p-1)/2}<\ldots<-x_{2}<-x_{1} are the negative zeros of Hp′H_{p}^{\prime}. Then due to the stronger result of Lemma 4.1, we have that |Hp​(x1)|=|Hp​(−x1)|<…<|Hp​(x(p−1)/2)|=|Hp​(−x(p−1)/2)||H_{p}(x_{1})|=|H_{p}(-x_{1})|<\ldots<|H_{p}(x_{(p-1)/2})|=|H_{p}(-x_{(p-1)/2})| with Hp​(xk)=−Hp​(−xk)H_{p}(x_{k})=-H_{p}(-x_{k}) for all k=1,2,…,(p−1)/2k=1,2,\ldots,(p-1)/2. Thus, there are exactly p−1p-1 distinct values for the local maxima and minima in the odd case. ∎

Remark 4.1.

It is well-known that (see, [28, Proposition 2.1]) target random variables Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) with h∈𝕂⁡[X]h\in\mathbb{K}[X] and deg​(h)=2\text{deg}(h)=2 admit a polynomial Stein operator of order two with linear polynomial coefficients.

Remark 4.2.

Part (c) of Proposition (4.1) is useful in implementing our code to find Stein operators for Hp​(X)H_{p}(X). In particular, if pp is even we must seek polynomial Stein operators with coefficients that have degree at least p/2p/2, and if pp is odd we require the degree to be at least p−1p-1. As can been seen in Table 1, we have used our MATLAB code to find polynomial Stein operators for HpH_{p}, p=1,…,10p=1,\ldots,10, that attain these minimum possible degrees. In fact, we have also tested this for p=11,12,14,16,18p=11,12,14,16,18, and our MATLAB code has always been able to find a Stein operator with the minimum possible degree. It therefore seems reasonable to conjecture that this is the case for all p≥1p\geq 1.

4.2 Examples of Stein operators for Hp​(X)H_{p}(X)

For univariate Gaussian polynomials, our MATLAB code can find all polynomial Stein operators up to a given order TT and maximum degree mm. We illustrate this in Appendix D by providing examples of Stein operators for Hp​(X)H_{p}(X), p=1,…,6p=1,\ldots,6, where X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). The code can also be applied to h⁡(X)h(X) when hh is not a Hermite polynomial, as demonstrated in the Supplementary Information (SI).

In this paper, we only give the ‘simplest’ Stein operators for Hp​(X)H_{p}(X), p=1,…,6p=1,\ldots,6. For p=1,…,6p=1,\ldots,6, we list the Stein operators with the lowest order TT and lowest degree mm (if there are two Stein operators with the lowest TT (mm), we given the one with lowest mm (TT)). For p≥7p\geq 7, the Stein operators become too complex to state in this paper, but in Table 1 we give a summary of the complexity of the ‘simplest’ Stein operators for p=1,…,10p=1,\ldots,10. Many other examples are given in the SI, some of which are ‘simpler’ in other senses than those presented in Appendix D, such as having lower values of T+mT+m or T×mT\times m.

The Stein operators in Table 1, except the one for H9​(X)H_{9}(X) with (T,m)=(9,40)(T,m)=(9,40), were obtained using a standard laptop, a MacBook Pro with processor: 2,9 GHz Dual-Core Intel Core i5 and memory: 8 GB, 2133 MHz, LPDDR3. Despite the complexity of the operators, the code found them rather quickly. For example, it was able to find the horribly complex Stein operator for H9​(X)H_{9}(X) with (T,m)=(41,8)(T,m)=(41,8) in just 343.3​s343.3\,$\mathrm{s}$. We easily obtained the Stein operator for H9​(X)H_{9}(X) with (T,m)=(9,40)(T,m)=(9,40) using a powerful computer server at The University of Manchester, and, whilst not explored in this study, a full exploitation of such computational power could yield some hugely complex Stein operators! Indeed, using just a standard PC, we obtained a Stein operator for H20​(X)H_{20}(X) with zero-order term c​y​f​(y)cyf(y) and (T,m)=(11,54)(T,m)=(11,54), with 402.6 CPU and elapsed time 4276​s4276\,$\mathrm{s}$.

There are several interesting observations we can make from the Stein operators presented in Appendix D and the summary in Table 1. We notice that there is an important increase in complexity from p=1,2p=1,2 to p=3,4p=3,4, in which the Stein operators go from being first order with linear coefficients (for which it is simple to solve the corresponding Stein equation) to be being at least second order with higher order coefficients (for which we are not able to solve the corresponding Stein equation). There is a further increase in complexity from p=3,4p=3,4 to p=5,6p=5,6, in which the Stein operators go from being expressed in one line equations to equations that sprawl several lines.

From Table 1, we observe that, for 0-order term c​y​f​(y)cyf(y) the ordered pairs (T,m)(T,m) satisfy the following recipes:

  • (a)

    Minimum TT: (i) when p≥4p\geq 4 is even, we have (T,m)=(p/2+1,(p/22)+p/2−1)(T,m)=(p/2+1,{p/2\choose 2}+p/2-1); (ii) when p≥3p\geq 3 is odd, we have (T,m)=(p+1,(p2)+(p−1)/2−1)(T,m)=(p+1,\binom{p}{2}+(p-1)/2-1).

  • (b)

    Minimum mm: (i) when p≥2p\geq 2 is even, we have (T,m)=((p/2+12),p/2)(T,m)=(\binom{p/2+1}{2},p/2); (ii) when p≥3p\geq 3 is odd, we have ((p+12)−(p−1)/2,p−1)(\binom{p+1}{2}-(p-1)/2,p-1).

For general 00-order term we have:

  • (c)

    Minimum TT: (i) when pp is even, just pick up the pair (T,m)(T,m) minimizing mm with 00-order term c​y​f​(y)cyf(y) associated with that value of pp and switch the components; (ii) when pp is odd, pick up the pair (T,m)(T,m) minimizing TT with 00-order term c​y​f​(y)cyf(y) associated with that value of pp and set (T−1,m+1)(T-1,m+1).

  • (d)

    Minimum mm: for both even and odd pp this is the same as in item (b).

Rather curiously, the minimum values of TT seem to be connected with the number of distinct local maxima and minima of the Hermite polynomial HpH_{p}. We know that this is the case for the minimum possible degree mm, due to Proposition 4.1, part (c).

We observe that for each pp we tested the code always found a Stein operator with the minimum possible degree (see Proposition 4.1, part (c)). We do not, however, have a proof of an analogous result for the minimum possible order TT of Stein operators. In theory, it is therefore possible that we have not actually found Stein operators with the minimum possible values of TT. However, our tests suggest that this is a remote possibility. For example, for zero-order term c​y​f​(y)cyf(y), our code could not find any Stein operators for H4​(X)H_{4}(X) with input variables T=2T=2 and m=60m=60, nor for H5​(X)H_{5}(X) with input variables T=5T=5 and m=80m=80. Additionally, we performed many other tests with our code and verified all of the predicted recipes (a) – (d) for a number of values of pp between 11 and 20 (the complex Stein operator for H12​(X)H_{12}(X) is given in the SI). As such, we believe that it is reasonable to conjecture that the recipes (a) – (d) hold for all pp.

Appendix B Auxiliary lemma

Lemma B.1.

Fix d=1d=1. Let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). Assume that g⁡(X),h⁡(X)∈𝕂⁡[X]g(X),h(X)\in\mathbb{K}[X] with 𝕂=ℚ,ℤ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Z}. Then with Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X),

𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)|h⁡(X)=y]=0,∀y∈supp⁡(Y)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[g(X)\,\big|\,h(X)=y\big]=0,\quad\forall y\in\mathrm{supp}(Y)\; (B.1)

if and only if one of the two conditions below are satisfied:

  1. (a)

    g≡0g\equiv 0, i.e., gg is identically the zero polynomial.

  2. (b)

    gg is an odd polynomial and hh is an even polynomial, meaning that g⁡(−x)=−g⁡(x)g(-x)=-g(x) and h⁡(x)=h⁡(−x)h(x)=h(-x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

Note that (B.1) is equivalent to

∑x∈ℝ:h⁡(x)=yg(x)e−x2/2=0,∀y∈supp(Y).\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\mathbb{R}:h(x)=y}g(x)e^{-x^{2}/2}=0,\quad\forall y\in\mathrm{supp}(Y). (B.2)

Next we discuss on the degree of polynomial hh. Suppose first that hh has odd degree, in which case hh is not an even polynomial. Then for all yy with |y||y| large enough the algebraic equation h⁡(x)=yh(x)=y has one and only one real root, let us say r⁡(y)r(y), and moreover the mapping y↦r⁡(y)y\mapsto r(y) is strictly monotone outside a compact interval. Then relation (B.2) yields that the polynomial gg has infinitely many real roots, which implies that g≡0g\equiv 0.

Now, consider the case with hh of even degree. Then, for all |y||y| large enough, depending on the signs of yy and of the leading coefficient of hh either equation h⁡(x)=yh(x)=y has no real roots or it has only two real roots, let us say r1​(y),r2​(y)r_{1}(y),r_{2}(y) so that r1​(y)<0<r2​(y)r_{1}(y)<0<r_{2}(y). Moreover, as before the mappings y↦r1​(y),y↦r2​(y)y\mapsto r_{1}(y),y\mapsto r_{2}(y) are strictly monotone outside a compact interval. Next assume that g≢0g\not\equiv 0. In the latter case relation (B.2) means that for all large enough yy:

g​(r1​(y))g​(r2​(y))=−exp⁡(r2​(y)2−r1​(y)22).\displaystyle\frac{g(r_{1}(y))}{g(r_{2}(y))}=-\exp\biggl(\frac{r_{2}(y)^{2}-r_{1}(y)^{2}}{2}\biggr). (B.3)

Now, by choosing y∈ℚy\in\mathbb{Q}, the roots rj​(y)r_{j}(y), j=1,2j=1,2, of the algebraic equations h⁡(x)=yh(x)=y, are algebraic numbers (because 𝕂=ℤ,ℚ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q}), and hence the left-hand side of relation (B.3) is an algebraic number since the quotient of two algebraic numbers is again an algebraic number. This implies that the right hand side of relation (B.3) is an algebraic number and that in virtue of the Lindemann-Weierstrass theorem [11, Theorem 1.4] this only happens when r2​(y)=±r1​(y)r_{2}(y)=\pm r_{1}(y). But our sign justification yields that must be r1​(y)=−r2​(y)r_{1}(y)=-r_{2}(y) for all large enough y∈ℚy\in\mathbb{Q}. Therefore, from the relation (B.3) one can infer that g⁡(r2​(y))=−g⁡(r1​(y))g(r_{2}(y))=-g(r_{1}(y)) for all large enough y∈ℚy\in\mathbb{Q}. Now consider polynomial G⁡(x):=g⁡(x)+g⁡(−x)G(x):=g(x)+g(-x). Then, this polynomial would have infinitely many roots, and hence G⁡(x)=0G(x)=0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, i.e., gg is an odd polynomial. Looking to a new polynomial H⁡(x):=h⁡(x)−yH(x):=h(x)-y, and with a similar argument one can conclude that h⁡(x)=h⁡(−x)h(x)=h(-x) for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, i.e., hh is an even polynomial. ∎

Supplementary Information

Appendix C MATLAB implementation

This appendix is devoted to a concise description of the implementation of the null controllability approach in MATLAB to find polynomial Stein operators for Gaussian polynomial distributions of the form Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) in the univariate case (d=1)(d=1), for which our code returns many new polynomial Stein operators. Some of them are listed in Appendices D and E. Our exposition in this appendix mostly focuses on polynomial Stein operators of the form

𝒮=∑t=0Tpt∂t\mathcal{S}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}\partial^{t}

having zeroth-order term p0​(y)=c​yp_{0}(y)=cy for some constant cc. These are often the most useful Stein operators, in particular, in the context of the Nourdin-Peccati Malliavin-Stein approach. In Remark C.1, we describe how the implementation of our code is modified for generic zeroth-order coefficients p0​(y)p_{0}(y).

The body of the MATLAB code consists of the following:

(a)

Input variables: the code requires the following three input variables,

  • •

    Polynomial h=h⁡(x)∈𝕂⁡[x]h=h(x)\in\mathbb{K}[x]; this input variable corresponds to the target distribution Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X), a Gaussian polynomial random variable with X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). We further assume that the polynomial hh is chosen in a such way that I​E​[Y]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[Y]=0. Prototypical examples are h=Hph=H_{p}, the Hermite polynomials with p≥1p\geq 1.

  • •

    Variable TT stands for the maximum time horizon to check the null controllability, and corresponds to order of the polynomial Stein operator. The program starts checking the null controllability with t=1t=1 onwards until t=Tt=T, and stops at step tt as soon as it finds a null control sequence. Otherwise, the code returns with an error in the case there is no a null control sequence of the maximum length TT. In that case, one has to enlarge the time horizon.

  • •

    Variable mm is the maximum degree of the null control sequence (pt(y):t=0,…,T)(p_{t}(y)\,:\,t=0,\ldots,T) in the target variable yy, i.e. m=maxt=0,…,T⁡deg⁡(pt)m=\max_{t=0,\ldots,T}\deg(p_{t}). In the language of algebraic geometry, the input variable mm yields the control state to be 𝕂m​[y]\mathbb{K}_{m}[y] (Remark 3.7, item (ii)). Again, the code returns with an error in the case there is no a polynomial null control sequence with maximum degree mm. In that case, again, one has to enlarge mm.

⬇
1 %%% input variables %%%
2 h=h(x);
3 %%% corresponds to the target Gaussian polynomial Y= h(N) with E[Y]=0, for example h=hermite(4,x) %%%
4 T=10; %%% time horizon %%%
5 m=4; %%% maximum degree of polynomial coefficients of Stein operator in the target varaible y=h(x) %%%
(b)

Output variables :

  • •

    Vector uu= [c,u] stores the coefficients of the polynomials (pt:t=0,…,T)(p_{t}:t=0,\ldots,T) of the found Stein operators. This output variable is useful when degree of the input polynomial hh is large, translating to Hermite polynomials h=Hph=H_{p}, when pp is large. This enable us to observe semi-directly the polynomial coefficients of the found Stein operator, and avoid the printing since it is quite time consuming.

  • •

    Variable t in the workspace assigns the order of the found Stein operator.

  • •

    Variable m1 in the workspace assigns the maximum degree of the polynomial coefficients associated to the found Stein operator.

  • •

    The end-part of the code is devoted to the printing of the found Stein operator in LaTeXas well as the symbolic format ∑t=0Tpt​(y)​Dt\sum_{t=0}^{T}p_{t}(y)D^{t}. This is done through the output variable stein_eq.

(c)

Pseudocode for the null controllability problem :

The following Pseudocode constitutes the main body of the code. It consists of two parts. The first part implements in a recursive method the crucial relation (3.10) to find a null control sequence starting from t=0t=0 until t=Tt=T. The second part checks that the moment conditions () are satisfied. As above, input variable TT is the upper bound on the order of the Stein operator, Λ\Lambda is the control matrix and Γ\Gamma is the evolution matrix. Nmoments is the vector I​E​[Xk]k≥1{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[X^{k}]_{k\geq 1}, v0v_{0} is the coefficient vector of the given zeroth-order polynomial term p0​(h​(x))p_{0}(h(x)) in the independent variable xx satisfying I​E​[p0​(h⁡(X))]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(h(X))]=0. For example, when h=H4​(x)=x4−6​x2+3h=H_{4}(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+3, and p0​(y)=c​yp_{0}(y)=cy, then v0=c⁡(3,0,−6,0,1)v_{0}=c(3,0,-6,0,1).

Remark C.1.

The algorithm above for a given target Y=h⁡(X)Y=h(X) takes as input the zeroth-order polynomial coefficient p0​(h​(x))p_{0}(h(x)), with I​E​[p0​(h⁡(X))]=0{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[p_{0}(h(X))]=0. In order to find a Stein operator with generic p0​(y)p_{0}(y) we run the algorithm several times with the respective initial coefficients p0(k)​(y)=yk−I​E​[h​(X)k]p_{0}^{(k)}(y)=y^{k}-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}[h(X)^{k}], in order to obtain the corresponding Stein operators satisfying

I​E​[𝒮(k)​f​(Y)]=−I​E​[p0​(Y)​f​(Y)]\displaystyle{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[{\mathcal{S}}^{(k)}f(Y)\bigr]=-{\rm I\kern-1.60004ptE}\bigl[p_{0}(Y)f(Y)\bigr]

for k=1,…,m0k=1,\dots,m_{0}. When the Stein chains end successfully and Stein operators are found for the initial coefficients above, by solving a linear system for the linear combination one can further reduce the order or the maximal coefficient degree of a Stein operator with a generic zeroth-order polynomial coefficient p0​(y)p_{0}(y) of degree ≤m0\leq m_{0}.

Appendix D Stein operators for univariate Gaussian Hermite polynomials

The Stein operator for H1​(X)H_{1}(X) is the classical standard Gaussian Stein operator of [59]. The Stein operator for H2​(X)H_{2}(X) is a special case of the Stein operator for a​X2+b​X+caX^{2}+bX+c, a,b,c∈ℝa,b,c\in\mathbb{R}, of [28], as is the Stein operator for H1​(X)+H2​(X)H_{1}(X)+H_{2}(X) given in Appendix E. Also, the Stein operators (D.2) and (D.3) were already obtained by [28]. All other Stein operators in this appendix and Appendix E are new. Some of the Stein operators given in this appendix are also given in Appendix A. We repeat them here so that all the Stein operators are collected together in a single appendix.

Appendix E Ring operations and Stein operators

Our algorithm can also be applied to general univariate Gaussian polynomials. We collect some examples here, in which we consider linear combinations of Gaussian Hermite polynomials. In addition to this proof of concept, we are able to observe from our results that a small change in the target distribution can lead to substantial differences in the complexity of the Stein operators; see Remark E.1.

Remark E.1.

Stein’s method is rather sensitive to small perturbations in the target. Even a modest change in the target random variable YY can drastically change the original polynomial Stein operators in terms of the order (the length of null control sequence) as well as the maximum degree of the polynomial coefficients. For example, consider the target Y=−6​H2​(X)+H4​(X)=X4−3Y=-6H_{2}(X)+H_{4}(X)=X^{4}-3 that is obtained from the target random variable in item (f) via a multiplication by −6-6 of its first summand. For YY our code returns the following algebraic polynomial Stein operator of order two

y+(−32y−96)∂+(−16y2−96y−144)∂2.\displaystyle y+(-32y-96)\partial+(-16y^{2}-96y-144)\partial^{2}.

A similar example of this type is the target Y=H3​(X)+3​H1​(X)=X3Y=H_{3}(X)+3H_{1}(X)=X^{3} with algebraic polynomial Stein operator (compare with (D.1) and (D.2))

y−15∂−81y∂2−27y2∂3.\displaystyle y-15\partial-81y\partial^{2}-27y^{2}\partial^{3}.

In contrast, consider the target variable Y=H4​(X)+H1​(X)Y=H_{4}(X)+H_{1}(X) in item (e) that is perturbed by a copy of the underlying standard Gaussian random variable XX. One can observe a drastic change in the complexity of the original algebraic polynomial Stein operator (D.3) not only in the order but also in the maximum degree of the polynomial coefficients.
